title: Close attachment and process lifecycle races
description:
Contract routing:
- Hardens ORB-C1, ORB-C3, and ORB-C7.
- Preserves ORB-C2, ORB-C4, ORB-C5, and ORB-C6.
- Changes no product feature or compatibility boundary unless the user separately approves it.

Prove that attach, detach, client failure, child exit, server shutdown, signals, and socket cleanup have one bounded, idempotent Orbit owner. This Bead changes Orbit only; consumer UX findings are routed to Venus separately.
design:
Run after the transport-pressure child. Record the Execution baseline and pass the Reference gate before code.

Required before code: exact FrankenTerm session, reconnect, crash, and cleanup mechanisms; Process Triage observe-plan-apply, staged signal, reaping, and post-action verification mechanisms; zmx attach-ordering and restoration failures; and Qwertty raw-mode restoration and cleanup mechanisms. Foot 1.27.0 at de998602dbc00c8862a6823d553cbb1df91c676d is comparison only. Reject their remote, multi-session, controlling-terminal, fleet, and general cleanup scope.

Exercise aborted and simultaneous handshakes, deterministic second-client rejection, client crash, detached resize ownership, PTY EOF, foreground and known-child exit, server shutdown, signals, stale socket identity, and repeated cleanup. Use the existing platform seam and owned loop. Stop for a new process model, restart persistence, remote transport, new crate, or cross-repository correction.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Aborted, raced, and simultaneous attachment attempts preserve exactly one active client; rejection does not disturb the accepted client or PTY.
2. Client disconnect or crash leaves the live PTY/session available for coherent reattachment while Orbit remains running.
3. PTY EOF, foreground or known-child exit, server shutdown, and supported signals drain or discard owned state according to the indexed contracts without hangs or duplicate terminal actions.
4. Socket and platform resources are cleaned idempotently; stale identity cannot remove another listener or admit an unintended attachment.
5. Slow or failed lifecycle transitions use explicit synchronization and bounded timeouts and leave no abandoned client storage.
6. Orbit is the sole code owner in this Bead. Any Venus UX defect or boundary change is routed separately with exact revisions and compatibility order.
7. Closure reruns and updates or explicitly downgrades every touched ORB-C1, ORB-C3, and ORB-C7 proof and regression-checks preserved contracts.
8. Closure records portability, dependency footprint, owned LOC, exact verification, and remaining lifecycle limits. Restart persistence, multiple sessions, remote transport, and multiplayer remain excluded.
notes:
Accepted ownership: the one Orbit owner loop handles known-child exit by invoking the existing Pty cleanup owner before bounded final PTY materialization. Pty holds the live child as Option<Child>; cleanup takes Some to None before signaling and reaping, so later explicit or Drop cleanup is a no-op without an independent stopped flag. Cleanup always signals the owned child process group and any distinct foreground process group even after the leader exits, then kills and reaps the exact known child. Drop remains the fallback on other exits. Steady-state remains one PTY read per readiness turn.

After quiescence, Orbit consumes at most four PTY-master reads and stops earlier on closed/WouldBlock. The zmx measured Linux N_TTY maximum bounds this near 16 KiB. The real-PTY final-state regression emits 5,000 padding bytes before its final OSC title, requiring multiple reads and proving the reproduced final state reaches authoritative libghostty. The continuously writing inherited-PTY descendant regression proves bounded server exit, socket removal, and descendant cleanup. Excess raw output beyond the four-read post-exit budget is deliberately discarded when Pty drops; no client can attach after Exited.

Material rejected exit shapes: one final read lost the title; FIONREAD exposed only the current 4,095-byte chunk and missed later asynchronous PTY transfer; 4 MiB and 64 KiB drain caps let a live producer exceed the lifecycle deadline; stopping process groups followed by an unbounded finite-tail drain still flaked when debug libghostty materialization exceeded five seconds. Quiescence plus the deterministic four-read budget is the smallest shape that preserves the reproduced multi-read final state and the hard shutdown bound. A separate stopped boolean was rejected because Option<Child> directly represents whether cleanup ownership remains.

ORB-C3 negotiation, invalid ordering, simultaneous rejection, abort recovery, and canonical reattachment share one strong lifecycle test. Client holds negotiation_deadline: Option<Instant>; Some means awaiting Hello until the existing one-second deadline and None means attached. This removes the independent attached/timestamp invariant. Other peers receive Busy while negotiation is live; expiry closes the abandoned socket and releases the slot without disturbing the PTY. The canonical validation client retries Unix-socket I/O and pre-attachment Busy responses within its existing five-second deadline. Canonical decode and ordering errors fail immediately: Attached is accepted exactly once, and duplicate Attached or Busy after Attached is rejected. Unbounded reservation, newest-peer eviction, duplicated server attached state, client-side ownership, a timer thread, and an async/state-machine framework were rejected.

The real-PTY detach proof observes PTY resize through the shell title and asserts retained 100x40 dimensions on the reattached client coherent initial frame. Shell PID continuity, deterministic Busy rejection, detached command completion, and owned cleanup remain co-located.

No wire protocol, dependency, manifest, platform abstraction, product boundary, timeout value, or attached-client behavior changes. Product Rust is 5,810 LOC, 64 lines over the prior accepted state. Portability disposition: neutral lifecycle, negotiation-deadline, and quiescence policy with Linux process groups, signals, PTY EOF, poll, and Unix sockets retained in the existing concrete platform seam.

Accepted proof revision 9e9b136969dc583d365daa75402ec03c265080f1 is compatible lifecycle hardening: ORBS v1, ORBF v1, orbit-protocol, manifests, dependencies, and valid client behavior are unchanged, so Venus requires no migration. title: Prove rich presentation fidelity on attachment and reattachment
description:
Contract routing:
- Hardens ORB-C4 and ORB-C6.
- Preserves ORB-C1 through ORB-C3, ORB-C5, and ORB-C7.
- Changes no product feature or compatibility boundary unless the user separately approves it.

Prove complete canonical frames preserve the accepted rich visible terminal state across attachment and reattachment without a formatter bootstrap, raw-byte replica, or client-owned emulator.
design:
Run after semantic input and resize hardening. Record the Execution baseline and pass the Reference gate before code.

Required before code: exact libghostty-vt render, row, cell, grapheme, cursor, title, hyperlink, screen, and capability surfaces; and zmx restoration failures showing why formatted text is insufficient. FrankenTUI deterministic scene-transition checks are comparison only here. Reject TUI cells, formatted-ANSI restoration, dirty-row patches, and client terminal emulation.

Exercise primary and alternate screens, styled Unicode, combining and wide graphemes, resolved backgrounds, cursor shapes and visibility, title, hyperlinks, complete-frame revision order, coherent replacement on reattach, resize, and explicit unsupported capability reporting. Stop for graphics, effects, history, patches, protocol revision, dependency, or Venus correction.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Complete frames preserve accepted styled graphemes, combining and wide-cell roles, resolved colors, cursor, title, hyperlinks, screen state, and explicit capabilities.
2. Attachment and reattachment materialize one coherent complete state followed by strictly ordered revisions with no stale final presentation.
3. Alternate-screen transitions and resize remain semantically equivalent without formatter restoration, raw PTY replay, or a client terminal emulator.
4. Supported rich state is never silently collapsed to plain text, and unsupported graphics or effects remain explicit rather than partially invented.
5. Focused checks use canonical frames and authoritative state and distinguish protocol fidelity from native Venus rendering quality.
6. Orbit is the sole code owner; any Venus or boundary defect is routed separately with exact revisions and compatibility order.
7. Closure advances or explicitly downgrades ORB-C4 and ORB-C6 at an exact proof revision, regression-checks preserved contracts, and records portability, dependency footprint, LOC, exact verification, and remaining capability gaps.
notes:
Accepted state

Ownership and code shape: Orbit remains the sole terminal-state and presentation owner. ORBF v1, the extractor, runtime, protocol, and client boundary require no production change. The existing real_pty_reattach_converges_through_complete_ordered_frames test is the single proof owner.

The proof drives one live shell into a resized 80x30 alternate screen and checks the canonical frame for exact default and palette colors; hyperlink; RGB foreground, resolved background, underline color, bold, italic, faint, blink, inverse, invisible, strike, overline, curly underline, and protection; a combining grapheme; wide head and spacer-tail roles; a background-only erased cell; hidden steady-underline cursor state; title; working directory; active screen; hyperlink support; and explicit absence of Kitty graphics. A second client receives a byte-decoded frame exactly equal to that complete rich revision. After the deterministic release changes authoritative state, the next attached initial frame is strictly newer than the rich revision; any following frames are also strictly ordered. The pressure phase preserves final primary-screen convergence after a slow client, semantic interrupt, split CSI, UTF-8, and APC input.

Simplification disposition: keep the single real-pipeline proof. Helpers, expected-frame fixtures, split matrices, and weaker aggregate assertions add machinery or lose field-level evidence without removing an owned concept. No production refactor is justified.

Rejected shapes remain formatter restoration, raw PTY replay, client terminal emulation, a second schema, graphical Venus claims, graphics or effects invention, history, patches, protocol revision, dependencies, and additional test matrices.

Proof lifecycle: the user accepted proof-bearing commit 847cab1ca37495c5cd45454623bd81909b488564. ORB-C4 and ORB-C6 advance to that immutable revision in docs/CONTRACTS.md. ORB-C1 through ORB-C3, ORB-C5, and ORB-C7 are preserved by unchanged production code and the passing canonical suite.

Dependencies and LOC: Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, and docs/CRATES.md are unchanged; the ten-package normal graph remains. Product Rust source and tests are 6,027 lines, up 70 test-only lines; governance is 765; total owned Rust is 6,792. No production LOC changed.

Portability: neutral presentation/protocol result with the live PTY proof isolated to the existing Linux runtime test surface. No macOS blocker, support claim, or cross-repository compatibility change is introduced.

Accepted Linux evidence for exact commit 847cab1ca37495c5cd45454623bd81909b488564: cargo fmt --all --check; cargo check --locked --workspace; cargo test --locked --workspace with 47 tests; cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .; Starcompass 95c29fa check-consumer; cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings; git diff --check; and the focused real-PTY proof ten consecutive candidate runs. title: Measure the accepted Orbit-Venus boundary under real workloads
description: This is the final no-code acceptance slice for orb-bi4.5. It changes no product contract. Consume the exact accepted Orbit and Venus proofs and measure the real one-client boundary under representative terminal workloads. Route every confirmed defect to its single owning repository and Bead instead of repairing it inside this measurement run.
design:
Run only after transport pressure, lifecycle, and terminal-semantic hardening close. Pin the exact ORB-C1 through ORB-C7 and VEN-C1 through VEN-C4 proof revisions being exercised.

Before the first workload run, record the exact machine, display stack, window and grid size, commands, sampling method, and explicit numeric pass/fail ceilings. The envelope must cover p50 and p95 input-to-present latency when externally observable, idle CPU and RSS, sustained-output CPU and RSS, extraction time, encoded bytes per frame and per second, queue replacement, Venus apply or rebuild time, resize-storm convergence, and final-state convergence. A metric that cannot be observed without production instrumentation is marked unavailable before the run; do not silently replace it with an internal proxy.

Dogfood an ordinary shell, Neovim, Yazi, resize storms, and high-volume output. Use existing diagnostics or external observation. If meaningful measurement needs production instrumentation, a public trace, an adapter, or a dependency, stop and route that capability separately.

The result makes one decision. If the predeclared envelope passes, accept complete ORBF frames for the pre-graduation dogfood path and retain snapshots as the resynchronization fallback. If it fails, identify the limiting stage and route one owner correction; propose dirty-row extraction or snapshot-plus-row-patch only when extraction, encoding, transfer, or complete-scene application is the measured limit. This task may append factual evidence and update planning or contract documentation after accepted proofs, but it must not edit Orbit or Venus production code, tests, or manifests.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Before measurement, record the exact Orbit and Venus proof revisions, consumed contract IDs, machine and display environment, workload commands, observation method, and numeric pass/fail ceilings.
2. The declared envelope covers p50 and p95 input-to-present latency when externally observable, idle CPU and RSS, sustained-output CPU and RSS, extraction time, encoded bytes per frame and per second, queue replacement, Venus apply or rebuild time, resize convergence, and final-state convergence. Unobservable metrics are declared before the run with the missing observation surface.
3. Shell, Neovim, Yazi, resize-storm, and high-volume-output runs record the declared measurements against identical named conditions rather than incomparable anecdotes.
4. Detach, client loss, and reattachment preserve coherent current state during representative workloads and expose bounded visible failure behavior.
5. The result states one evidence-backed outcome: complete frames pass the envelope for pre-graduation dogfood, or the boundary is a no-go pending one routed owner correction. Passing does not claim that patches are never needed.
6. A failed metric identifies the limiting stage before proposing a remedy. Dirty-row extraction or snapshot-plus-row-patch is proposed only when measured extraction, encoding, transfer, or complete-scene application cost is causal.
7. Measurements distinguish observed facts from inference and do not promote visible-only dogfood into history, effects, graphics, platform, or restart-persistence proof.
8. Every confirmed defect is routed to one owning Orbit or Venus Bead with compatibility order where needed; no production code, test, manifest, adapter, dependency, or new trace surface changes here.
9. The result records the still-separate history and ordered-effect gaps. orb-bi4.5 reconciles the accepted child proofs, measurements, decision, and remaining risks before closure.
10. orb-bi4.6 remains blocked until this task and orb-bi4.5 close.
notes: Measured no-go at Orbit 847cab1 and Venus 8149002. All declared functional and lifecycle workloads passed, but sustained output exceeded the combined CPU ceiling: p95 240 percent versus 200 percent. External attribution was Orbit 101 percent and Venus 141 percent p95. Routed one Venus-only correction as ven-39u. Complete frames and ORBS v1 remain accepted contracts but are not accepted for pre-graduation dogfood until the correction passes this exact envelope. History orb-j0m, ordered effects orb-ll1, and graphics orb-j2i remain separate.
close_reason: Measurement complete: sustained-output CPU is a no-go at combined p95 240 percent versus the 200 percent ceiling; routed the single owner correction to Venus Bead ven-39u.

title: Choose post-graduation Eon, Venus, and Orbit ownership boundaries
description:
After a go in orb-bi4.8, choose exactly one post-graduation implementation frontier and its cross-repository order. Preserve Orbit as generic terminal-session authority, Venus as native materializer and interaction owner, and Eon as agent-first workspace, product policy, orchestration, composition and distribution owner. On a no-go, close this Bead as not applicable.

Product direction:
Agents are strategically central to Eon. The user selected eon-pxn as the single post-graduation implementation frontier: an Eon-owned workspace model that treats AgentRun as explicit product identity and maps it to repositories or worktrees, provider identities, services, artifacts, execution targets and independent Orbit sessions. Its user-selected first native topology is a fixed two-axis surface: horizontal tabs and a visual vertical accordion pane stack with direct directional traversal and no virtual pane picker. This decision establishes ownership and order without activating implementation or another frontier.

Narrow-waist rule:
1. Keep an agent independent from a pane, PTY, process, Orbit session, provider thread and Venus view.
2. Keep process and terminal truth in Orbit, provider-native semantic evidence in an explicit integration, normalized AgentRun and attention policy in Eon, and native presentation in Venus.
3. For cross-boundary behavior compare no protocol change, an existing bounded plane and the smallest explicit extension in that order.
4. Keep snapshots or patches, history, effects, resources, actions, agent observation and product control as distinct responsibilities.
5. Every extension names one benefit, owner, consumer, numeric bounds, authorization, cancellation, compatibility, portability, proof and total LOC/runtime cost.
6. Keep exact-revision lockstep while Orbit and Venus are the only accepted pair. Add no public protocol, shared schema repository, compatibility window, generalized negotiation, plugin ABI or provider framework without an independently approved need.
7. Accept one vertical slice before another. Reopen architecture rather than accumulate adapters when coordination or duplicated truth becomes disproportionate.
design:
Current ownership:
- Orbit owns PTYs, terminal state, terminal viewport, selection, copy text, process/session lifetime and generic terminal identity.
- Venus owns frame materialization, native gesture collection, window geometry, focus, accessibility and platform clipboard or launch side effects. It owns no terminal viewport or history truth.
- Eon owns workspace topology and product policy: repositories or worktrees, AgentRuns, services, artifacts, execution-target references, launch and resume policy, secrets policy, component relationships and mappings to Orbit session identities.

Agent state remains source-aware. Orbit can prove process/session lifecycle, not provider intent. Provider semantic state is accepted only from an explicit integration. Eon may compute attention from fresh accepted evidence and must show unknown when semantic evidence is absent. Venus displays Eon state without scraping terminal content.

The first agent-workspace slice should compare no machine-readable surface with a deterministic local CLI or existing local socket for stable-ID list, tab and pane creation, directional or identity focus, attach, start, wait, explicit stop, and view removal distinct from session termination. Bounded terminal observation remains a separate read-only capability owned through orb-p92. MCP may later adapt accepted Eon actions; it is not the first protocol, plugin system or authorization owner.

For eon-pxn, the chosen bounded Eon workspace composes multiple independent one-session Orbit endpoints as one product slice: Eon owns horizontal-tab and per-tab vertical-pane order, Venus materializes a visual accordion with one expanded pane and persistent collapsed headers, and direct workspace commands traverse tabs left or right and panes up or down without a picker. This does not authorize an Orbit multi-session process or give Orbit layout ownership.

Decide an Orbit process that hosts multiple sessions separately from Eon workspace topology, restart recovery separately from detach, remote terminal transport separately from web/mobile presentation, and remote environment orchestration separately from all three. Effects, search, semantic regions, observation and graphics remain separate candidates. Select exactly one frontier.

Accepted decision and update order:
1. Activate the minimum eon-pxn Eon owner for stable tab and pane identities, ordered topology, independent Orbit-session mappings, and only the semantic actions required by that topology.
2. Activate a separate Eon-owned managed interactive-environment child under eon-pxn. Eon owns its selected components, exact identities, private configuration, command projection, and product defaults; the tools retain native behavior and schema ownership.
3. Activate the Venus consumer for opaque horizontal tabs and the one-expanded vertical accordion. Orbit remains unchanged unless an exact owner-contract gap is found.
4. Prove the cross-repository dogfood workspace.
5. Only after the opaque workspace passes, separately activate the minimum Venus appearance capability for Eon-owned font, theme, bell, and default-background opacity policy.

The full managed-environment decision lives in eon-pxn. Orbit only launches the exact selected argv and retains process, PTY, terminal, and session authority; it does not own Nushell, prompt, editor, file-manager, Git UI, PATH, alias, theme, font, bell, or opacity policy. Opaque tabs do not wait for a general configuration system, plugin mechanism, observation plane, effects framework, remote support, or native Eon editor. A missing prerequisite pauses the frontier at its real owner rather than inviting a Venus or Orbit workaround.
acceptance_criteria:
1. orb-bi4.8 records the graduation decision first.
2. After a go, every proposed expansion receives accept, reject or defer with one repository owner.
3. eon-pxn is the selected single next frontier because agents are strategically central to Eon. Its accepted first topology is horizontal tabs plus per-tab visual vertical accordion panes, one expanded pane at a time, direct directional traversal and no ordinary vertical pane picker.
4. The selected agent-workspace contract keeps AgentRun distinct from pane, process, PTY, Orbit session, provider thread and Venus view.
5. Ownership preserves Orbit terminal, viewport, selection and copy authority; Venus native presentation and interaction; and Eon workspace, AgentRun, action and attention policy without duplicate truth.
6. Process lifecycle, provider semantic state and Eon attention state have explicit separate sources. Unknown semantic state is never guessed from terminal output, titles, timing or process names.
7. Any first Eon action surface compares no API with a minimal deterministic local CLI or existing socket for stable-ID list, tab and pane creation, directional or identity focus, attach, start, wait, explicit stop, and view removal distinct from session termination. It separates read-only observation from mutating actions; MCP, plugins, pane pickers, raw terminal control and provider-specific actions remain separate decisions.
8. Eon composition of multiple independent one-session Orbit endpoints and its bounded horizontal-tab plus visual-accordion topology travel together under eon-pxn. An Orbit process hosting multiple sessions, simultaneous expanded panes, arbitrary or durable layouts, virtual pane pickers, floating terminal popups, restart recovery, state patches, effects, search, semantic regions, observation, graphics, remote attachment, web/mobile clients and remote machines remain separately decidable slices.
9. Each accepted responsibility defines its user contract, known consumers, exact update order, authorization, bounds, cancellation, proof, portability, LOC and maintenance before implementation planning.
10. Exactly one implementation frontier is selected; all others remain deferred.
11. Separate repositories remain the default. A monorepo, shared schema repository, compatibility layer, new protocol owner or provider framework requires explicit user approval.
12. Eon and Nova remain independent.
13. On a no-go, this Bead closes as not applicable without speculative cleanup or planning scope.
14. The selected implementation order is the minimum Eon topology and action owner; a separate Eon-managed interactive-environment child; the Venus opaque horizontal-tab and one-expanded vertical-accordion consumer; cross-repository dogfood acceptance; and only then a separately approved Venus appearance child. Broader AgentRun/provider semantics, declarative profiles, terminal observation, MCP, plugins, isolation, generalized APIs, and effects remain outside the first workspace slice unless a required owner-contract gap blocks it.
15. eon-pxn is the sole owner of the accepted managed-environment details and Eon product defaults. Orbit receives exact launch inputs but gains no shell, tool, PATH, configuration, font, theme, bell, or opacity policy.
16. Tabs and accordion panes prove opaque composition first. Default-background opacity is later Venus capability work under a separately approved VEN contract, while the 0.92 product default and immediate 1.0 override remain Eon policy. A missing prerequisite returns to its owning repository before the frontier continues.
notes:
Selected frontier: P1 Eon agent-first workspace eon-pxn. Deferred alternatives remain P1 phased read-only agent observation orb-p92; P1 Orbit effects separation orb-ll1; P2 search orb-qcc; P2 semantic command regions orb-3gf; P3 graphics orb-j2i; P1 Venus hyperlink interaction; and P2 Venus structured accessibility. This decision activates no parallel implementation.

At activation, eon-pxn creates separate Eon owner, any required Orbit owner, Venus consumer and acceptance children. No implementation children are created by this planning correction.

User topology decision on 2026-08-07: keep the first workspace deliberately two-axis and visible. Tabs traverse horizontally; panes form a visual vertical accordion with one expanded session and bounded persistent headers. Ordinary up or down pane traversal does not open a picker. This is Eon/Venus product topology over independent Orbit sessions, not an Orbit layout or multi-session contract.

Exact current Herdr, Amp Orbs and VS Code Agent Host material informs agent-workspace and client-independent execution mechanisms only. Canario remains the compact workspace cost comparator. No reference is a dependency or compatibility target.

First-slice sequencing clarification (2026-08-08): eon-pxn is the product frontier. Eon first owns stable tab and pane identities, ordering, independent Orbit-session mappings, and only the semantic actions required by the slice; a separate Eon child proves the managed interactive environment; Venus then materializes opaque horizontal tabs and the visual accordion; cross-repository dogfood accepts the result. Do not build the complete AgentRun/provider model, declarative profile, observation, extension, isolation, or generalized API horizon before this workspace proof, and do not let Venus compensate for a missing Eon contract.

Decision completed by user on 2026-08-08: select eon-pxn and its owner-first order. The Eon topology/action owner precedes the separately scoped managed interactive environment; Venus then consumes the topology as opaque tabs and accordion panes; cross-repository dogfood follows; appearance comes later. eon-pxn records the accepted Nushell, Starship, Zoxide, Helix, Yazi, LazyGit, managed-command, private-PATH, manifest, theme, font, bell, and opacity policy. Nova revision `37f36efcabf16c41d03e182917926e7b8e56139c` is comparison evidence for that Eon-owned plan only. Carapace, automatic Direnv or Mise activation, command-alias configuration, cursor effects, general configuration, plugins, observation, and generalized APIs stay deferred. No implementation child or product contract is created by this closure.

Future Eon Web direction selected by the user on 2026-08-10: use a TypeScript browser shell, compile the canonical Rust Orbit protocol decoder and client-state reducer to WebAssembly, and use Effect as the default browser-side lifecycle runtime for typed transport failures, resource scopes, cancellation, bounded concurrency and streams, scheduling, reconnect, and deterministic substitution in tests. Plain browser code retains DOM, ARIA, input, clipboard, rendering, and PWA ownership. Effect does not decode ORBF or ORBS, own terminal state, render the terminal, define remote authorization, or become an Eon-wide plugin or schema framework. Agent-assisted development velocity is an accepted reason not to reject the stronger lifecycle model merely for unfamiliar syntax, learning cost, or initial implementation effort; exact ownership, lifecycle correctness, security, dependency health, bundle and runtime cost, and replacement cost still govern adoption. This selects the future default shape but activates no web contract, remote transport, repository, dependency, or implementation.

title: Decide whether Venus and Orbit earn Eon graduation
description:
Decision gate: decide whether the proven Venus and Orbit pair earns the Eon implementation frontier after hardening, minimum native history, scrolling, selection and copy, and fresh Eon dogfood that includes one real coding-agent lifecycle. This Bead changes no runtime contract or implementation.

Required evidence:
- Exact accepted ORB-C and VEN-C proofs, revisions, compatibility order, platforms and every remaining P0 or P1 owner gap.
- The accepted workload envelope and the native-history end-to-end LOC, latency, CPU, memory, request, failure-state and compatibility evidence.
- Fresh native dogfood demonstrating whether client-independent process lifetime, coherent reattachment, one terminal authority and explicit failure ownership are materially valuable for ordinary terminal work and for one bounded real coding-agent task.
- A refreshed Canario comparison with separate distribution and mechanism evidence. Use `canarioterm/releases` commit `fcadcfeea7e337114d28beec0e0cbe89493a654d` and release `v2026.08.07.15`, built from private revision `canario@af91699`, for distribution evidence. Use Rio `ff8efcc4ad0359889de44b1baacea7014cdada30`, the final public Canario tree before extraction commit `e69b5fffef25abd5e649bf4ac205636551e54482`, for inspectable same-process lifetime and restoration mechanisms. Treat current private internals as unknown.

Protocol-gravity falsification:

notes:
Graduation decision

User decision: GO on 2026-08-08. Advisor confidence: 80 percent. Venus and Orbit earn graduation as the Eon foundation. This decision changes no product contract, proof revision, runtime, dependency, repository boundary, distribution channel or follow-up implementation.

Accepted proof set

- ORB-C1 through ORB-C9 are Proved at Orbit `9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757`; ORB-C10 is Proved at `292b2451c9a1d99390334771a681c7f481c996f2`. Orbit distribution revision `00b136318bea13e3f08d490468f069de6f6b9bd2` preserves them.
- Venus `2d36c72dc87ca5416e22d6afdc35c6ab4e2fb832` consumes the exact ORBF v1 and ORBS v2 owner package. VEN-C1, VEN-C2, VEN-C3, VEN-C4 and VEN-C7 are Proved at their indexed revisions. Venus materializes frames, captures native input, exposes accessibility and clipboard effects, and owns no PTY or terminal model.
- Eon manifest proof `c9e898c9ff889c2be4d4381a20676291bab65b49` pins Orbit `00b1363` and Venus `2d36c72`. EON-C1 proof `712c0834691c58b07e56494de25f98670b6a882e` and EON-C2 through EON-C4 composition proof `eae70e8d3ed4348b389f320dfd49d7db29478546` establish the accepted Nix-only Linux composition. EON-C5 through EON-C7 remain planned distribution work and carry no foundation correctness claim.
- The owner-first ORBS v2 change landed in Orbit, then Venus pinned the exact revision, then Eon pinned the accepted pair. No adapter, duplicate schema, feature probe, dual decoder or compatibility window exists.

Demonstrated value

Closed orb-bi4.6 consumed a fresh Eon run with Codex CLI 0.147.0 in a disposable Rust repository. Venus exited while Codex was active. Eon, Orbit, the PTY and Codex survived; `eon attach` opened a new Venus against the same session; the task completed; and independent format, test and Clippy checks passed. Provider semantic state remained unknown. The same component pair exercised 3,000 history rows, rapid wheel input, return to live, wrapped Unicode, wide-grapheme selection and copy, resize and reflow, Helix, Neovim, Yazi keyboard and application mouse, DEC 1007, output pressure, client loss and coherent reattachment.

The corrected sustained-output envelope passed at combined CPU p95 167 percent under the declared 200 percent ceiling, peak combined RSS 55.3 MiB and final convergence 13.6 ms. The native history proof completed 32 synchronous wheel round trips in 39.620976 ms with a 12,809-byte complete ORBS frame. The real-pair lifecycle proof observed coherent reattachment in 122 ms. These measurements retain their named workloads and do not become broad performance claims.

ORBF v1 carries styled graphemes, colors, cursor, title, working directory, hyperlinks, active-screen identity and explicit capability flags. Orbit owns retained history, viewport, selection and copy; Venus never reconstructs terminal state from text or PTY bytes. The accepted capability set preserves rich state without a visible-screen or text-grid ceiling. Kitty graphics remain declared unsupported.

Protocol and ownership cost

Orbit added 57 production and 370 test lines for authoritative viewport behavior. Selection and copy raised product Rust and tests from 6,454 to 7,161 lines, a further 707 lines. Current Orbit accounting is 7,183 product Rust lines, 765 governance Rust lines and two terminfo lines. The dependency-free `orbit-protocol` package owns 3,100 Rust lines, including 2,131 production and 969 test lines.

The accepted Venus history, selection, copy and accessibility slice changed 835 net Rust lines from its pre-slice baseline and added arboard 3.6.1 behind the native clipboard seam. Arboard required 15 Venus production lines and 12 all-target lock packages. Current Venus accounting is 4,359 Rust source lines, 363 integration-test lines and 5,301 tracked handwritten lines. Eon keeps one component manifest and launch owner; its current scorecard includes 1,026 Rust source and test lines.

At the exact comparison revisions, Eon, Orbit and Venus contain about 12,931 tracked Rust lines across their scorecards. Nova `cf313431ca0b08352b0a5b4b0beb2341aee5568a`, Mars `2b63717135a72ef330d8c2da8ca4cde59c22d739` and Yazelix Zellij `bbccdea6eda81f314151160f9b3f8882a26478ec` contain about 521,170 tracked Rust lines. These raw maintenance surfaces do not equate feature sets, but the gap supports the smaller ownership conclusion. Nova remains an independent product because Eon still excludes its layouts, plugins and multi-session workspace behavior.

Comparator result

Canario publishes builds through `canarioterm/releases` commit `fcadcfeea7e337114d28beec0e0cbe89493a654d`; release `v2026.08.07.15` records private source `canario@af91699`. Current private internals remain unknown. Rio `ff8efcc4ad0359889de44b1baacea7014cdada30`, the final public tree before extraction `e69b5fffef25abd5e649bf4ac205636551e54482`, remains the inspectable integrated comparator. It keeps PTYs in the application, restarts shells and restores layout, CWD, title and text scrollback. That shape has lower protocol cost but fails the selected live-process survival contract.

Herdr main `3a76fea2d858a7a5ef58615f1cc9aabaa30b80ee` and stable release `v0.8.0` publish a server/client contract for durable agent terminals and transient clients. Herdr also owns workspaces, multiple panes, restart restoration, remote attachment, agent heuristics, integrations, plugins and an agent API. Graduation accepts its process-continuity lesson and gives zero credit to those broader surfaces.

The Canario integrated shape cannot satisfy ORB-C1, and Herdr corroborates the value of a separate durable terminal owner. Neither reference justifies compatibility or adoption. Complete frames remain accepted because the measured envelope passed; patches, dirty-row extraction and a second renderer remain deferred.

Risks and limits

The audit found one approved protocol exception: orb-bi4.2 comment 14 records the user's 2026-08-04 one-time authorization to reconstruct baseline, reference and crate-gate evidence after those timing rules were adopted during the candidate. The exception applies only to orb-bi4.2, does not claim the records predated implementation, and does not extend to another Bead. Later accepted proofs reran the canonical checks.

No known P0 or P1 correctness blocker remains. Open or deferred P1 items are decision or feature scope: orb-bi4.7, agent observation, ordered effects, Venus hyperlinks and Eon workspace planning. Linux/Nix and Xwayland carry the accepted proof. macOS, native Wayland quality, candidate-list IME quality, proprietary NVIDIA packaging, direct distribution and restart persistence remain unproved. One synthetic wheel delta of 80 disconnected Venus, while representative rapid unit input passed and reattachment recovered. Optional emoji and Yazi icons showed fallback boxes. Search, effects, graphics, richer selection, multiple sessions, layouts, remote transport, web and mobile remain separate decisions.

The selected dependency cost remains material: libghostty-vt 0.2.1 builds pinned Ghostty `a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083` through Zig, the source checkout measured about 155 MiB, Venus carries a native GPU, shaping and accessibility stack, and the Eon Nix closure is about 1.46 GiB. Exact lockstep across three repositories remains a maintenance cost. Dogfood, bounded failure ownership and the smaller maintenance surface justify that cost at this stage.

Two nonblocking metadata discrepancies remain outside this authorized planning-only run: the Orbit crate index retains an obsolete sentence that Venus still consumes ORBS v1 until `ven-4sn`, and Venus VEN-C3/VEN-C4 rows retain historical partial-ORB-C7 wording against their original consumed proof despite the current Eon pair pinning proved ORB-C7. The canonical current consumer relationship in Orbit and Eon contract indexes is correct.

Decision consequence

Graduation unblocks orb-bi4.7 to choose exactly one post-graduation frontier. This run creates no implementation bead, starts no frontier, changes no changelog and does not promote a distribution channel. Nova remains unchanged.

title: Extract the canonical ORBF v1 codec for Venus
description: Create the smallest Orbit-owned, platform-neutral Rust protocol surface that lets Orbit and Venus consume one canonical ORBF v1 interpretation at exact revisions without changing the accepted wire contract.
design: Add one dependency-free orbit-protocol package inside the Orbit workspace. It owns ORBF v1 version and bounds, canonical frame data, bounded decode and validation, byte encoding, and complete-frame revision reduction. The existing Orbit server consumes the package while libghostty extraction remains in Orbit; Venus later consumes the exact same package from a pinned Orbit Git revision. Preserve ORB-C4, ORB-C6, and ORB-C7 behavior and byte compatibility. Do not add a new wire version, public trace format, fourth repository, crates.io publication, renderer, raw PTY path, terminal state, schema generator, or external dependency.

4. Orbit presentation extraction uses that package and emits byte-compatible frames without changing ORB-C4 or ORB-C6 behavior.
5. Decoder checks reject bad magic, unsupported versions, truncation, trailing bytes, invalid tags/flags/dimensions, allocation-hostile lengths, and stale or regressing revisions within explicit bounds.

10. Touched proved contracts remain partial until an accepted proof-bearing commit, then ORB-C4 and ORB-C6 advance to that exact revision; ORB-C7 remains honestly partial unless its full hardening gap is closed.

comments.text:
Crate gate — accepted dependency and package decision — 2026-08-04

Decision already authorized by the user after the protocol-boundary stop: add one internal, dependency-free, platform-neutral orbit-protocol workspace library and make yazelix-orbit depend on it by path. Do not add an external crate, publish target, schema generator, compatibility window, fourth repository, or second decoder. This gate records the comparison behind that accepted choice; it does not expand the approval.

Affected contracts: ORB-C4, ORB-C6, and ORB-C7; Venus will consume the exact accepted Orbit Git revision for VEN-C1 through VEN-C4. Existing product dependencies remain libc 0.2.189 and libghostty-vt 0.2.1 in the root binary only.

Candidate matrix:

1. Selected — internal std-only orbit-protocol package with the existing explicit little-endian ORBF v1 codec.
Fit/ownership: exact fit; one format owner, reusable by Orbit and Venus, no PTY/terminal dependency leakage, no wire revision. Estimated code movement is the existing roughly 60-line encoder plus roughly 100-line test decoder, with owned public values, errors, reducer, and focused tests added in the same package; no duplicated schema. Cost: one direct workspace path edge, zero external direct/transitive/native/build/Nix dependencies, no proc macros, no generated files. API/versioning: private Git-pinned package, publish=false, explicit VERSION=1 and strict errors; Orbit controls upgrades with its proof commit. License/security: project-owned; checked arithmetic and pre-allocation bounds can match the exact hostile-input contract. Platform: std-only byte/value logic is neutral across Linux, macOS, and a future wasm32 consumer. Accessibility/input/browser: no policy or OS API is embedded, so those remain consumer concerns.

2. Root library target with terminal features, no new package.
Fit/ownership: can expose a decoder but couples consumer resolution to the yazelix-orbit package and its libc/libghostty build graph unless terminal dependencies become optional features. That feature split adds manifest states and makes it easier for protocol and terminal ownership to drift within one crate. Project LOC is superficially smaller but consumer/build isolation is worse. Rejected because the acceptance criterion requires a consumer build that cannot compile PTY, libc, libghostty, or governance code.

3. Keep the encoder private and hand Venus a separate decoder.
Fit/ownership: zero dependency cost but creates the forbidden second schema and makes byte drift invisible until cross-repository integration. Rejected by the Orbit/Venus ownership contract.

4. bincode 2.0.1, MIT (the crates.io latest, 3.0.0, is a deliberately nonfunctional compile_error placeholder and is not a credible candidate).
Fit: mature general Rust binary codec, but its derived representation is not accepted ORBF v1; preserving v1 would still need the owned parser/encoder. Default 2.0.1 adds bincode_derive and unty, with proc-macro/build graph; serde is another optional edge. Owned LOC is not removed for the existing format. Pure Rust and broadly portable, but upgrades/configuration become wire decisions. Rejected: dependency cost and format instability for zero contract gain.

5. postcard 1.1.3, MIT OR Apache-2.0.
Fit: compact/no_std serde format, but it changes bytes and needs serde plus cobs and default heapless support; preserving ORBF again leaves a custom adapter. Pure Rust, macOS/wasm credible, no native dependency, but its embedded-oriented framing and serde data model do not prove the terminal-specific bounds or exact accepted revision. Rejected: more transitive and upgrade surface without removing the canonical codec.

6. prost 0.14.4 / Protocol Buffers, Apache-2.0.
Fit: mature schema evolution and multi-language ecosystem, but ORBF v1 is not protobuf. It adds bytes and prost-derive at runtime and normally prost-build plus a .proto/generated source workflow at build time; that increases build, cache, Nix, and upgrade surfaces and creates generated artifacts. Browser interoperability is strong in a different protocol, but no remote or general multi-language protocol is authorized. Rejected: wire change, generator, schema compatibility surface, and materially greater cost.

7. rkyv 0.8.17, MIT.
Fit: high-performance archive/zero-copy model, but archived Rust layout, alignment/pointer-width choices, validation, and its broad dependency set are unnecessary for a small bounded network frame and make cross-target stability a larger concern. Defaults include bytecheck plus derive and supporting crates such as hashbrown, munge, ptr_meta, rancor, and rend. No native build is required, but compile/upgrade/security review cost is highest of the pure-Rust candidates. Rejected: no measured zero-copy pressure, wrong stability shape, changes bytes.

8. capnp 0.27.0 / Cap’n Proto, MIT.
Fit: explicit schema and cross-language evolution, but requires a new wire and generated bindings; normal development adds capnpc/schema compilation and may require the external capnp tool, creating build and Nix/platform cost. It is credible for a future separately approved multi-language/remote protocol, not for exact v1 extraction. Rejected.

9. Separate protocol repository/package publication.
Fit: strongest physical isolation but adds a fourth version/release/coordination surface and conflicts with the accepted exact-Git-revision consumption model. Rejected by the user-approved scope.

Focused proof and disputed claims: cargo info and normalized crates.io manifests were inspected for bincode 2.0.1/3.0.0, postcard 1.1.3, prost 0.14.4, rkyv 0.8.17, and capnp 0.27.0. bincode 3.0.0 contains compile_error!("https://xkcd.com/2347/"). The accepted e4fde443 Orbit source proves the existing format already has a compact encoder and test decoder, so an external serializer removes no required v1 logic.

Consequences of the accepted choice: Cargo.toml adds crates/protocol as a workspace member and orbit-protocol as a root path dependency; crates/protocol/Cargo.toml declares edition 2024 and publish=false with no dependencies. Cargo.lock should only gain the local package edge. docs/CRATES.md will record this durable decision. Root production maps libghostty state into protocol-owned values; the protocol crate never imports libghostty, libc, sockets, renderer APIs, platform APIs, or governance. The first check is an exact accepted rich-frame decode/re-encode plus bounded hostile-input and strict revision tests, followed by cargo tree/metadata evidence that orbit-protocol has no external dependency graph.

The codec is std-only with no cfg, OS, native, window, GPU, font, input-method, or accessibility API; it preserves a credible macOS and future separately authorized wasm32 consumption path without claiming either product target. title: Decide whether Orbit should retain its diagnostic client
description:
## Contract routing

This is a planning-only developer-surface decision. It changes no ORB product contract, executable behavior, CLI, documentation, or tests. Any chosen removal or relocation requires a separately authorized implementation Bead and explicit treatment of the existing public command spelling.

Consumer: Orbit maintainers debugging the canonical local session protocol; no current Eon or Venus runtime consumer is known.

Trigger: determine whether `yazelix-orbit client [SOCKET]` still provides unique diagnostic value after Venus and the real lifecycle/protocol integration suites became canonical consumers.

Result: record one evidence-backed decision to retain, shrink, relocate to test/example tooling, or remove the client, including the smallest surviving diagnostic path and all user-visible/doc consequences.

Important failures: do not infer zero external use only from local callers; do not remove the shared canonical codec; do not keep production CLI solely because it was useful before Venus existed.

## Why

The installed Orbit binary still exposes an interactive line-oriented diagnostic client. `run_client` connects and negotiates ORBS, converts each stdin line into Paste plus Enter, and prints server messages. The path is roughly 85 production LOC and appears unused by Eon, Venus, or the automated lifecycle suite, but it may remain the cheapest manual protocol probe.

Impact: LOW. Investigation effort: S. Decision risk: LOW. Confidence in removal opportunity: MED-HIGH.

## Evidence

- `src/main.rs:274-301`: public CLI dispatch exposes `client [SOCKET]` beside the production `serve` mode.
- `src/main.rs:546-628`: `run_client`, client-message writing, server-message reading, and diagnostic printing implement the interactive path.
- `README.md:13-25`: current product description still names the diagnostic client and canonical protocol use.
- `docs/RATIONALE.md:332-347`: historical sequencing retains a headless runtime and diagnostic client used by the initial proof.
- Repository search finds no Eon, Eonova, Venus, or Orbit test invocation of the installed `client` command; automated tests use their own typed fixtures/clients.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

- Record exact Orbit, Eon, Eon Desktop, and Eonova revisions inspected.
- Trace every local caller and documentation reference to the `client` command and its helper functions.
- Search known consumer repositories and package wrappers for invocation of `yazelix-orbit client`; distinguish absence in known sources from a compatibility promise to unknown users.
- Compare its unique debugging capability with `tests/lifecycle.rs`, protocol unit tests, Venus transport/integration tests, and ordinary socket/protocol fixtures.
- Check release/documentation history to determine whether the command is an accepted public surface, a developer-only experiment, or merely installed incidentally.

## Scope

In scope:
- `src/main.rs` CLI branch, `run_client`, and helpers used only by that branch.
- README/rationale/contracts/package references to the diagnostic client.
- Known Eon, Venus, Eonova, CI, and test consumers.
- Retain, shrink, test/example relocation, and removal shapes.

Out of scope:
- Editing runtime code, docs, tests, packages, or contracts.
- Removing or weakening the ORBS codec, server behavior, Venus attachment, or real lifecycle tests.
- Designing a new debugging UI, protocol inspector, TUI, logging system, or compatibility layer.
- Adding dependencies or a new published binary.
- Assuming support for unknown external consumers without evidence.

## Decision method

1. Inventory the exact production LOC/imports/branches owned only by the diagnostic client and any code shared with the server.
2. Inventory actual consumers and the unique troubleshooting questions the command can answer.
3. Compare four shapes: retain unchanged; shrink the existing command; move equivalent probing into test/example tooling; remove it and rely on canonical consumers/tests.
4. For each shape, assess installed surface area, maintenance with future ORBS changes, manual diagnostic utility, automated coverage, documentation cost, and compatibility risk.
5. Select the first sufficient shape; name exact retained capability, rejected alternatives, and the event that would reverse the decision.
6. If change is selected, specify the smallest later implementation slice and changelog/documentation obligations, but create no implementation Bead without separate user authorization.

## Acceptance

- Every local and known cross-repository consumer is accounted for.
- The record states whether `client` is a supported user-facing command, developer tool, or obsolete experiment and cites the evidence.
- Unique manual diagnostic value is demonstrated with a concrete workflow or rejected as already covered.
- The decision explicitly chooses retain, shrink, relocate, or remove and quantifies owned LOC/surface consequences.
- Any removal decision names the exact helpers/imports/docs affected and how maintainers perform the remaining necessary diagnosis.
- Any retain decision states why production CLI ownership is cheaper than existing test/example mechanisms.
- The Bead records rejected alternatives, compatibility limits, reversal conditions, and whether later implementation is warranted.

## Verification

- `rg -n 'run_client|Some\("client"\)|yazelix-orbit client|diagnostic client' README.md docs src tests .github Cargo.toml` should enumerate all local references.
- Equivalent searches in the checked-out Eon, Eon Desktop, and Eonova repositories should enumerate known consumers.
- `cargo test --locked --workspace` should establish the current canonical protocol/lifecycle baseline; it does not by itself prove the interactive command unused.
- If retained value is claimed, record one exact manual workflow and its observed unique signal without modifying repository state.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0; implementation and documentation files must remain unchanged.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue for this Bead.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only authorized planning state.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if a known runtime, CI job, or supported external workflow consumes the command and removal policy needs a user compatibility decision.
- Stop if the command or ORBS revision changes during investigation; record the new snapshot and restart the analysis.
- Stop if evaluating an alternative requires source edits or a new diagnostic feature.
- Stop if removal would weaken canonical server, protocol, or lifecycle verification.

## Maintenance notes

Do not replace 85 production LOC with a similarly sized custom example. If automated tests already answer the necessary questions, deletion is the smallest shape; if live manual probing is genuinely unique, retain the production command deliberately.
notes:
Decision — 2026-08-14: remove the installed diagnostic client in a separately authorized implementation Bead. This decision changes no product contract and makes no runtime, documentation, test, or manifest edit.

Classification: the client is a documented proof-era developer probe, not a supported product command. It was introduced with the first PTY-lifetime proof; Eon packages the binary but invokes only serve, Venus consumes canonical ORBS directly, Eonova consumes the packaged composition, and no known runtime, package, test, or CI path invokes client. The private repository has no tags, releases, or forks.

Selected shape: delete the client CLI arm, client-only BufRead and BufReader imports, run_client, and print_server_message; reduce the usage text to serve. The current branch and client/helper/printing region is about 82 source lines: about 62 client-only lines can disappear, while write_client_message and read_server_message remain useful to strong tests and should become test-only rather than be duplicated. Update current README and rationale wording, preserve or clarify only necessary historical contract wording, and record the user-visible command removal in CHANGELOG when accepted. The implementation changes no ORB contract but touches the shared owner surface, so it must classify and reprove ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 as preserved.

Why: the exact live probe accepts a socket, maps every stdin line to Paste plus Enter, and prints attachment, acknowledgements, failures, exit, and frame revision/size/title. It does not print terminal cells or the submitted shell output, cannot express most accepted semantic messages, mutates the session, and occupies the sole client slot. Venus is the complete live manual consumer. The canonical lifecycle and presentation tests provide stronger deterministic negotiation, input, detach/reattach, state, failure, and rich-frame signals.

Rejected: retain unchanged keeps obsolete installed and protocol-coupled surface; shrink keeps the same command/compatibility burden for less signal; relocation replaces the deleted code with a similarly sized example and duplicates existing typed test clients.

Maintainer diagnosis after removal: use cargo test --locked --test lifecycle shell_survives_detach_and_one_client_reattaches -- --exact for lifetime and reattachment, cargo test --locked --bin yazelix-orbit presentation::tests::real_pty_reattach_converges_through_complete_ordered_frames -- --exact for rich state, the broader canonical suite for protocol/failure questions, and Venus for live manual attachment. Reconsider a dedicated tool only after a concrete live-server question cannot be answered by Venus, tests, or normal process/socket diagnostics.

No implementation Bead is created by this decision; user authorization is required.
close_reason: Decision complete: remove the obsolete proof-era diagnostic client in a separately authorized implementation Bead; retain canonical test clients and Venus as the diagnostic paths.

title: Decide Orbit same-boot session hosting and adoption
description:
## Problem

Orbit e60554623d2ad1e238fac84d0f8f49be0e81e522 already survives loss of its graphical client, but it is launched and observed as a std::process::Child of the Eon supervisor. Orbit owns the real PTY and authoritative libghostty state; Eon owns the product Session mapping and lifecycle policy.

This leaves a precise same-boot gap. If Eon exits normally, current stop paths terminate Orbit. If Eon crashes without running cleanup, Orbit may remain as an orphan with a live Unix socket, but a replacement Eon cannot safely prove that the endpoint belongs to the expected Session and generation, observe its authoritative exit, obtain its exit status, stop it through an accepted owner, or distinguish it from stale or replaced state. A PID, pathname, or filesystem record is not process identity.

Decide the minimum process-hosting and local management shape required for a replacement Eon to reconnect to the exact still-running Orbit Session after Eon supervisor loss. This is not machine-restart persistence, topology reconstruction, remote attachment, or multiplayer.

## Contract routing

- This is a deferred decision/research Bead. It changes no ORB-C, EON-C, or VEN-C contract, reserves no contract ID, and authorizes no code, binary, daemon, service unit, dependency, protocol, or packaging change.
- The Eon product decision eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf must first select exact same-boot supervisor-loss continuity.
- If selected, approve and index the smallest user-visible Orbit lifecycle/management contract before implementation. Preserve ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 and the one active presentation client.
- Orbit remains the only PTY process, terminal-state, retained-history, terminal-query, and Session-lifetime authority. Eon remains product identity, topology, selection, and recovery-policy owner. Venus remains transient.
- Keep management identity/status/stop distinct from ORBS presentation attachment. Do not weaken the one-client rule merely to let Eon inspect a live Session.

## Evidence

Current owner flow:

- src/main.rs::run_server creates the local listener, owns Pty and libghostty Terminal, exits on shutdown signal or PTY completion, and removes its exact socket on drop.
- src/platform.rs::Pty creates a new session and controlling PTY for the child; dropping Orbit sends HUP/KILL to the child process groups and reaps the direct child.
- Eon f036f798855668b53fa7e099fcb938ba6f0ffe2f stores every Orbit process as Child, observes it with try_wait, and owns normal stop and workspace pruning. Workspace and Session IDs are in-memory.
- ORBS proves presentation attachment, Busy, exact socket identity during startup, coherent frames, and detach/reconnect. It does not prove management identity, adoption by a new Eon parent, Orbit restart, or machine restart.

Relevant comparisons:

- zmx 4f3739ef98f44d0b639afa57fd76bffcad5d0ef4 and abduco 8c32909a159aaa9484c82b71f05b7a73321eb491 use one daemon/server per session. Per-session failure isolation is useful; their raw-terminal bootstrap, multi-client behavior, command surfaces, labels, and session semantics are rejected.
- shpool 901e18c3ced010073178b78c0ca2a8cdd43e8581 uses one daemon retaining child ownership and ships systemd socket/service units plus macOS launch-service guidance. Its shared daemon is comparison evidence, not an adopted dependency or architecture.
- tmux 851c5a933d4838c32ad06c248b2ba975d106149c uses one background server and stable in-server IDs; official docs state sessions are gone if the server is killed. This demonstrates both clean parenting and the shared failure domain.
- systemd 40315add9176d2a7c28d8d90490f74e9e982e87b can own transient or persistent user services and track their cgroups. loginctl linger can keep the user manager running after logout. This is credible Linux ownership but creates a platform and product-policy seam.
- CRIU is irrelevant to the first decision: the process is already alive. No checkpoint or terminal-state serialization should enter this scope.

## Proposed scope

Compare the mechanism options, recommend one or no change, and define the first contract check. Every option must cover authoritative identity, start convergence, useful-work survival, exit observation, explicit stop, socket recreation or replacement, stale metadata, permissions, version mismatch, partial startup, crash cleanup, logout behavior, and Linux/macOS removal cost.

Out of scope: persistence after Orbit or machine restart; topology or launch-intent storage; remote transport; SSH; cloud sync; history export; graphics; multiple clients; a public protocol; process checkpointing; automatic adoption based only on PID/path/process name; and implementation.
design:
## Options to compare

### Option A — no new behavior

Keep the Eon supervisor as the only launcher/parent and promise durability only while it remains alive. This is the smallest system. Improve diagnostics and wording in the Eon decision, but add no Orbit surface.

### Option B — systemd user service per Orbit Session

Eon requests a transient or generated user service with a stable opaque Session/run identity; systemd owns process and cgroup lifetime, while Orbit remains PTY authority. Eon validates owner-authored Orbit identity before attach and uses service-manager status/stop through one platform seam.

Advantages: mature Linux supervision, crash-independent parenting, bounded start/stop and logs, no project-owned generic daemon. Costs: systemd user-manager availability, linger and runtime-directory policy, unit cleanup, command or D-Bus integration, Nix packaging, Linux-only behavior, and a credible macOS replacement. Do not make a systemd unit name the product Session identity.

### Option C — one portable Eon session broker

A long-lived local broker becomes the parent and wait owner for all Orbit processes; replacement Eon supervisors query it through a private bounded control boundary.

Advantages: correct child exit/status ownership, portable conceptual model, one management endpoint. Costs: new binary/process/protocol, all-Sessions shared failure domain, broker upgrade and restart semantics, resource bounds, and potential duplication of Eon lifecycle ownership. The broker may host processes but must not own terminal or product topology state.

### Option D — self-daemonizing per-session Orbit

Each Orbit process detaches safely from Eon, retains direct PTY-child ownership, and exposes a narrow private management identity/status/stop plane. Replacement Eon discovers candidates, validates exact owner-authored identity, and reconciles them.

Advantages: per-session failure isolation, no shared broker, closest to current one-process-per-Session shape and zmx/abduco evidence. Costs: daemonization/stdio/signal semantics, stable run identity, management concurrency, endpoint recreation, non-parent exit observation, logs, cleanup, and platform launch differences. Do not stretch ORBS presentation negotiation into a second client or let filesystem metadata become authority.

### Option E — Linux pidfd adoption without a durable owner

A replacement Eon validates a run record, opens a pidfd, polls for exit, and signals it through the Linux platform seam.

Potentially small on Linux, but it cannot by itself recover wait-owned exit status and remains vulnerable to incomplete identity/record authority. macOS needs another mechanism. Treat it as a focused primitive inside another accepted shape, not a default product architecture.

### Option F — PID file, process-name scan, or socket-only adoption

Reject. PID reuse, same-path replacement, version mismatch, and stale sockets make these unsafe lifecycle authorities. Files may locate a candidate only; a live owner-authored handshake must validate it.

## First proof shape if selected

Use one isolated Session running a deterministic long-lived command. Kill the Eon supervisor with SIGKILL without signaling Orbit. Start the exact accepted replacement control path, validate the same run and Orbit identity, reattach through canonical ORBS, observe unchanged child PID and terminal state, then request owner-routed stop and prove bounded PTY-group cleanup plus no stale endpoint. Repeat with wrong identity, stale socket, incompatible generation, concurrent recovery, Orbit exit during recovery, and logout behavior. Machine reboot must fail the exact-continuity claim explicitly.

The decision must name the cheapest platform-neutral contract and the narrow Linux process/platform seam.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The final comparison covers no change, per-Session systemd user services, one portable broker, self-daemonizing per-session Orbit, pidfd as a subordinate Linux primitive, and unsafe PID/path adoption.
2. Each viable option assigns one owner for launch, stable run identity, live validation, child exit and exit status, explicit stop, socket lifecycle, normal shutdown, supervisor crash, Orbit crash, abandoned Session cleanup, and version mismatch.
3. Orbit remains sole PTY and terminal-state authority; Eon remains product Session/topology/recovery-policy authority; Venus receives no persistence responsibility.
4. Management and presentation remain separate logical responsibilities. The one active ORBS presentation client is preserved, and no consumer reconstructs terminal state from raw PTY bytes or files.
5. Candidate discovery is non-authoritative until a live owner-authored handshake validates stable Session identity, unique run identity, exact protocol/component generation, process start identity, endpoint identity, and user ownership. PID, socket path, process name, or stored metadata alone cannot authorize attach or stop.
6. The decision defines bounds for startup, handshake, retries, clients, queues, logs, records, shutdown, partial failure, and cleanup, plus permissions and symlink defenses.
7. Every viable option records portability as neutral, isolated platform dependency, or macOS blocker with exact replacement shape and estimated removal cost. systemd and pidfd remain behind a narrow Linux seam.
8. The first proof kills Eon while useful work continues, reattaches a replacement to the same process and authoritative terminal state, then proves owner-routed stop. Negative checks cover stale/replaced endpoints, wrong identity, concurrent recovery, incompatible generation, Orbit exit, and machine reboot.
9. The recommendation names dependency and binary impact, owned LOC estimate, upgrade/removal cost, and evidence that would reverse it. Prefer no new crate and no new process unless the contract cannot be satisfied otherwise.
10. The user approves no change or one mechanism before any contract-index, code, manifest, package, or service-unit edit.
notes:
Planning-only batch authorized on 2026-08-12. No implementation, baseline, Reference gate comment, or Crate gate is required or implied by this decision record.

Priority P2 and deferred. The initial evidence favors comparing Option D against Option B, with Option A as the baseline: per-session ownership fits Orbit failure isolation, while systemd is the strongest Linux native supervisor. A shared broker is justified only if exact exit/status and lifecycle ownership cannot be expressed cleanly per Session.

Required before any later implementation decision: reread AGENTS.md, eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf, exact current Eon lifecycle source and accepted EON-C8/EON-C10/EON-C11 proofs, ORB-C1 through ORB-C11, docs/REFERENCES.md PTY/session-lifetime routing, exact current FrankenTerm lifecycle evidence, zmx, shpool, abduco, tmux, and systemd source.
