comments.text:
Decision evaluation and approval gate — 2026-08-19 America/Sao_Paulo

Scope and prerequisite

- This planning-only evaluation changes no ORB-C, EON-C, or VEN-C contract and authorizes no implementation, crate, binary, service unit, package, or protocol.
- The prerequisite is not yet satisfied. `eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf` remains deferred and explicitly awaits the user selection required by its AC9. Its notes recommend same-boot continuity first but do not accept that behavior. Therefore this Bead cannot honestly close or authorize a mechanism yet.
- Smallest candidate contract, if the user selects it: after abrupt Eon supervisor loss on the same boot and login while Orbit remains alive, a replacement Eon may discover a candidate, validate the exact live Orbit run through an owner-authored handshake, acquire the sole management lease, and attach through canonical ORBS to the unchanged PTY and authoritative terminal state. Wrong, stale, replaced, incompatible, incomplete, or already-ended candidates fail closed. Closing Venus remains ORB-C1 detach; explicit Eon generation stop remains destructive owner-routed stop; logout, reboot, machine loss, and Orbit loss do not preserve the process.

Exact evidence inspected

- Current Eon `827c30faec1f58159fc2a335d6a17a6567c55d3f`: `RunningSession` stores Orbit as `std::process::Child`; Eon alone polls exit, holds in-memory topology, and kills/waits Orbit during explicit stop. Startup waits five seconds for a new socket identity. Current EON-C8, EON-C10, and EON-C11 evidence validates only the live supervisor and generation.
- Current Orbit `5a2c7e03aea770f752dd467be7975dbb44aabd07`: Orbit already owns the PTY child wait status, authoritative libghostty state, ORBS, and ORB-C12 contained stop. ORB-C1 preserves the live Session across graphical-client loss. It has no management identity or replacement-supervisor lease.
- zmx `9575587bbe363a6652c17d64d002c67eb1f32e6a` and abduco `8c32909a159aaa9484c82b71f05b7a73321eb491`: one server per terminal session owns the PTY, reaps the child, and survives client loss. abduco retains the child status while its server remains available. Their labels, PID recovery, raw-terminal protocol, and multi-client semantics are rejected.
- shpool `b7486f0ed9f29d940f077495424b7e1a6ade2864` and tmux `6696151008847cf354a89470742d72f5c8c3160b`: a shared server gives a clean wait owner but creates one all-Sessions failure domain and a new long-lived protocol owner.
- FrankenTerm `78fefc6b9b49ae674ea4aad3b76cdd23f16eb07e`: its daemon path separates stdio and session lifetime, while its documented persistence is bounded evidence/snapshot capture and explicitly does not continue the same process. This supports keeping process survival distinct from terminal/topology reconstruction.
- Linux man-pages 6.18 `pidfd_open(2)` and `waitid(2)`: a pidfd is stable and pollable/signalable, but `waitid(P_PIDFD)` returns `ECHILD` when the target is not the caller child. A replacement Eon cannot recover wait-owned exit status from pidfd alone.
- systemd v260.2 `f1d0952a125b96b7ab2f1ff29a87448ade8ac29b`: a per-Session transient service supplies supervision, cgroup membership, start/stop, and main-process status. However transient units are released when unreferenced; garbage collection loses exit results. Failed units can be retained, successful inactive results still need another retention owner. The current user scope is UID-owned and compatible with the existing ORB-C12 parent-cgroup permission check in the inspected environment. Linger is separate logout policy.
- Apple ServiceManagement and launchd documentation: a launch agent is the native macOS long-running replacement, requires application packaging/registration and user-visible policy, and receives termination at logout. It is not a zero-cost substitute for a Linux transient user service.
- CRIU, remote compute, terminal snapshots, raw PTY replay, and machine-restart recovery remain rejected scope.

Option comparison

A — No change. Viable if same-boot supervisor-loss continuity is not selected. Eon remains launcher, wait/status/stop owner and topology owner; Orbit remains PTY owner. Cost: zero code, crate, binary, package, and portability work. Exact Orbit survival after Eon loss remains accidental and unsupported; replacement Eon refuses adoption. This is the reversal if the Eon product decision stays deferred or rejects the guarantee.

B — systemd user service per Session. Viable Linux-native supervision, classified `isolated platform dependency`. systemd owns launch/process/cgroup/status/stop; Eon owns logical Session/run creation and recovery policy; Orbit still needs a live identity handshake and remains PTY owner. It does not eliminate the need for bounded successful-exit retention, stale endpoint validation, or an Orbit management identity. Logout survival requires the separate `linger` product policy. macOS replacement is an SMAppService-managed launch agent, with bundle, registration, consent, and logout semantics. Rough impact: no new crate or project binary; about 250–450 owned Rust lines plus Nix/service integration and cross-platform acceptance. Removal is medium because product startup and packaging become service-manager-shaped. Prefer this only if logout/start-at-login, administrator supervision, or service-manager operations become selected behavior.

C — Shared portable broker. Technically viable and mostly platform-neutral at the control layer. The broker owns launch, child handles, wait status, and stop; Eon owns product topology; Orbit owns PTY state. Cost: one new binary/process/private protocol and one all-Sessions failure/upgrade domain, roughly 700–1,200 owned lines plus proofs and packaging. It duplicates part of current Eon lifecycle ownership and is not needed merely to keep one already-self-owning Orbit alive. Reject unless a per-Session Orbit cannot provide authoritative status and a sole management lease.

D — Independently managed per-Session Orbit. Recommended if same-boot continuity is selected. Refine the label: do not double-fork or add a daemon launcher unless proof requires it. The current spawned Orbit already owns and waits for its PTY child. Eon may retain its `Child` handle while alive, but launch must use independent stdio and no parent-death coupling; after Eon SIGKILL the kernel may reparent Orbit without changing Orbit ownership. Add one private, versioned, bounded management endpoint and one owner-authored discovery/tombstone record. No new binary, service unit, direct crate, shared broker, or second terminal owner. Rough impact: 250–400 Orbit lines and 250–400 Eon lines plus focused owner/consumer proofs. Removal is low-to-medium: delete the private management surface and return to current parent-only supervision. Core identity/status messages are neutral; detachment, peer credentials, process-start identity, and optional pidfd checks are isolated platform seams. macOS needs equivalent spawn/stdio, peer-credential, and process-identity proof, estimated 150–250 platform/test lines; it is not a core redesign. Logout remains unsupported on both platforms.

E — pidfd. Useful only as an optional Linux subordinate primitive after a live handshake, for stable liveness or signal-handle cross-checks. It cannot own non-child wait status, logical identity, endpoint truth, history, or macOS behavior. About 100–200 isolated platform/test lines if later evidence justifies it; no standalone product mechanism.

F — PID file, pathname, socket inode, process-name scan, or stored record alone. Rejected. Each may locate a candidate; none authorizes attach or stop. PID reuse, endpoint replacement, stale files, incompatible generations, and same-user replacement make them unsafe authorities.

Recommended ownership and bounds for D

- Eon creates the stable logical Session ID and fresh opaque run ID and owns topology, selection, recovery policy, and whether an ended run is replaced. Venus owns no persistence.
- Orbit echoes and binds those IDs, owns the direct PTY child and exact exit status, exposes its exact component/protocol generation and OS process-start identity, and remains sole terminal/query/presentation owner. A live management handshake validates the expected IDs, peer UID, endpoint identity, process-start identity, and generation before any state-changing request.
- Management is separate from ORBS. One long-lived Eon management lease is allowed; disconnect releases it without stopping Orbit. Probes are read-only and bounded. Concurrent replacement Eons race for one lease; losers receive Busy. The existing one active ORBS presentation client is unchanged.
- Reuse the existing five-second startup/recovery operation ceiling and private runtime ownership. Limit candidate inspection to the existing 256-entry Eon ceiling. A management message is at most 4 KiB, IDs at most 128 bytes, error detail at most 1 KiB, and there is at most one request and response in flight per connection. No retry follows identity, ownership, or generation mismatch; transient connect attempts remain within the single five-second operation deadline.
- Use a 0700 UID-owned runtime directory and 0600 Unix sockets; reject symlinks, non-sockets, group/other-writable parents, wrong peer UID, and changed inode identity. Records are fixed-size locators only. Publish a live record atomically only after both management and ORBS endpoints are ready. A wrong or replaced live endpoint fails closed. Loss of a live endpoint is not repaired through PID signaling in the first contract.
- Orbit writes at most one bounded terminal tombstone for its run after reaping the PTY child, containing identity, exact status, and component generation, then removes its endpoints and exits. A tombstone may report that a known run ended but can never authorize attach or stop. It is removed when Eon reconciles it or the same-boot runtime directory ends. No process memory, terminal frames, scrollback, argv, environment, credentials, or topology are stored.
- Project-owned retained logs are zero. Independent stdio prevents Eon pipes from coupling lifetime; bounded diagnostics travel in the management response/tombstone. Add a retained log only after a demonstrated support need and a separate retention/privacy decision.
- Explicit stop goes only through the validated Orbit management lease. Orbit runs the existing bounded ORB-C12 shutdown, returns the direct-child result, removes exact endpoints, and terminates. If validation or connection fails, Eon reports non-success and does not fall back to PID, process-group, pathname, or cgroup killing.
- Eon crash preserves Orbit. Orbit crash loses the live Session and leaves only non-authoritative stale discovery state. Normal explicit Eon generation stop stops all validated managed Orbits. Graphical-client exit remains non-destructive. A process deliberately handed to another lifecycle manager is outside ORB-C12 containment; a hostile same-user program remains outside this lifecycle contract. Logout, reboot, and machine loss explicitly fail the continuity claim.

First proof and reversal conditions

Owner proof: start one deterministic long-lived PTY command, validate management identity, SIGKILL Eon without signaling Orbit, then prove the same Orbit PID/start identity, PTY child PID, terminal revision/state, and ORBS run remain live. Start two replacement Eons; exactly one acquires management while the other gets Busy. Attach through canonical ORBS, issue owner-routed stop, and prove the existing ORB-C12 containment becomes empty with no endpoint residue. Negative cases: wrong logical/run ID, stale and replaced sockets, wrong UID/mode/symlink, incompatible component/protocol generation, partial startup, Orbit exit during recovery, tombstone reporting without attach authority, management pressure, logout, and reboot. Implement in owner-first Orbit, consumer Eon, then cross-repository acceptance Beads only after contract approval.

Reverse D to A if the user does not select same-boot continuity. Reconsider B if logout/start-at-login or administrator service ownership becomes required, or if independent spawn cannot survive the accepted platform failure without a service manager. Reconsider C only if a per-Session Orbit cannot provide exact exit/status and sole-control leasing without becoming more complex than one broker. Do not adopt pidfd or filesystem metadata as a substitute for live owner identity.

Stop reason

Research converged, but AC10 and the Eon prerequisite require an explicit user choice. Recommended user decision: select phased durability with exact same-boot Eon-supervisor-loss continuity, and approve Option D in the reduced no-double-fork shape above. Until then, keep this Bead deferred and make no contract or implementation change.

title: Choose honest ORBS version-mismatch semantics
description:
## Contract routing

This is a planning-only compatibility decision. It changes no ORB product contract, wire bytes, implementation, dependency, or compatibility promise by itself.

Consumer: an exact local ORBS client and Orbit server that need deterministic behavior when their session revisions differ.

Trigger: compare the current exact-version header with the `Hello` version range and typed `Incompatible` messages before the next authorized ORBS revision.

Result: the user selects one coherent policy and owner: either keep exact-version framing and remove or narrow the unreachable range-negotiation surface in the next authorized breaking revision, or authorize a stable bootstrap envelope with explicitly bounded compatibility semantics. Record the update order for Orbit, Venus, and Eon/Eonova.

Important failures: do not silently add dual-version support, an adapter, a compatibility window, or a feature-probe framework; do not claim typed incompatibility when the peer cannot decode it.

## Why

ORBS v3 rejects a non-v3 header before decoding the `Hello` payload, yet the typed API advertises version-range overlap and `Incompatible`. A real v2 or future peer cannot reach that path or decode the v3 response. The current exact pin limits exposure but leaves dead compatibility flexibility and misleading failure semantics.

Impact: MED. Investigation effort: S. Decision risk: HIGH because the selected shape governs future wire compatibility. Confidence: HIGH.

## Evidence

- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:141-174`: `Hello` and `Incompatible` describe inclusive revision-range negotiation.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:572-597`: `message_len` rejects a header whose version differs from `VERSION` before message-kind or payload decoding.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:731-743`: the Hello range becomes available only after exact-header validation.
- `src/main.rs:653-672`: an actual header mismatch becomes generic `FailureCode::Protocol`.
- `src/main.rs:705-726`: typed `Incompatible` is reachable only for a current-header Hello whose payload range excludes v3.
- `tests/lifecycle.rs:455-470`: the incompatibility test uses the current encoder/header, so it does not exercise a stale or future header.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:110-119`: accepted v1-to-v2 and v2-to-v3 changes deliberately selected no adapter, dual decoder, feature probe, or compatibility window.
- Audit `orb-audit-orbit-protocols-bkk` recorded the issue at Orbit `7d34399b15496513f7f91b94acd32e8d04389e16`.

## Reference classification

Required:

- Current `AGENTS.md`, this complete Bead, `docs/CONTRACTS.md`, `docs/REFERENCES.md`, `docs/RATIONALE.md`, `docs/CRATES.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md`.
- Exact ORBS v1, v2, and v3 protocol sources and the accepted `orb-bi4.10`, `orb-j0m.3`, and `orb-ll1.1` decisions/proofs.
- Exact current Venus and Eon/Eonova pins plus their user-visible handling of protocol mismatch.
- Any then-active or selected next-revision protocol Bead, including `orb-orbit-typed-wheel-outcomes-5nq` and deferred `orb-j2i`, only to establish serialization and avoid conflicting revision ownership.

Comparison only:

- One or two mature local protocols with a stable bootstrap/version-negotiation envelope, if needed to falsify or specify that option. Record exact identities and adopt no surrounding transport, RPC, schema, or compatibility framework.

Rejected scope:

- Remote transport, capability negotiation, multiple simultaneous protocol decoders, indefinite backwards compatibility, a generic RPC handshake, or a new dependency.

## Scope

In scope:

- The current ORBS header, `Hello`, `Attached`, `Incompatible`, and protocol-failure flow.
- Known Orbit, Venus, and Eon/Eonova consumers and exact update ordering.
- A comparison of the minimum coherent policy shapes and their wire/LOC/test consequences.
- The first runnable check and a separately authorizable implementation slice if a change is selected.

Out of scope:

- Editing code, tests, manifests, docs, contracts, or protocol bytes.
- Choosing the next product feature or activating any open/deferred protocol feature.
- Implementing compatibility, adding a dependency, or creating implementation children before the user decision.
- Reworking non-version session messages.

## Decision method

1. Reproduce the exact mismatch: encode `Hello`, mutate only header bytes 4..6 to `VERSION - 1` while its payload range includes `VERSION`, and record that header validation prevents negotiation.
2. Trace what the exact current Venus client can decode or display for both older-server and newer-server cases.
3. Compare complete shapes:
   - retain exact-version framing and simplify the next authorized revision to exact `Hello`/attachment with header mismatch as a transport-level incompatibility;
   - retain the current range types as reserved but explicitly stop claiming cross-header negotiation;
   - define a stable minimal bootstrap envelope for future revisions, with exact support bounds and update order;
   - any smaller source-evidenced alternative.
4. For each shape, record public/wire semantics, decoder count, owned LOC, allocation bounds, failure UX, test surface, rollout order, removal cost, and interaction with already planned protocol revisions.
5. Recommend the first sufficient shape. Ponytail bias: exact pins plus the simplest honest failure surface unless a demonstrated supported workflow needs negotiable compatibility.
6. Stop for the user's explicit compatibility decision. If change is selected, specify one bounded Orbit-owner implementation Bead followed by separately owned consumer adoption; create neither in this run.

Portability disposition: neutral.

## Acceptance criteria

1. The current mismatch is reproduced with exact bytes and both peer directions are traced through the known consumers.
2. The record explains why today's typed `Incompatible` is or is not decodable by a different-header peer.
3. At least exact-framing simplification and stable-bootstrap shapes are compared without assuming a compatibility requirement.
4. The selected recommendation names one header/version owner, exact failure semantics, known consumers, update order, old-revision disposition, and whether it changes an indexed contract.
5. No adapter, window, second decoder, feature probe, dependency, or implementation is implied unless the user explicitly selects it.
6. The decision records rejected alternatives, reversal conditions, first falsifying check, effort/risk, and interaction with other planned ORBS revisions.
7. Repository files remain unchanged; only this Bead's planning record is updated.

## Verification

- `cargo test --locked -p orbit-protocol` should establish the current codec baseline.
- Run the focused byte-mutation reproduction in a disposable test/proof surface and record its exact result without editing production files.
- `rg -n 'Hello|Incompatible|UnsupportedVersion|client_message_len|server_message_len' crates/protocol/src/session.rs src tests docs` should enumerate local owners and claims.
- Exact searches in Venus and Eon/Eonova should enumerate consumers and mismatch UX.
- `cargo test --locked --workspace` should exit 0 on the unchanged decision subject.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0 with no implementation or documentation change.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only planning state.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if another active issue owns the same ORBS header/version decision.
- Stop if current source or consumer pins change; record a new subject and repeat the trace.
- Stop before any contract, protocol, code, test, manifest, or consumer edit.
- Stop if a compatibility promise, cross-repository update, or new dependency would be required without explicit user approval.

## Maintenance notes

This decision should be resolved before intentionally minting another ORBS revision, but it is not a blocker for read-only audits. Do not preserve range fields merely because they already exist; preserve only a demonstrated compatibility contract.

Rollout is Orbit proof → Venus exact-pin adoption → Eon component graph → Eonova Eon pin. Old revisions remain unsupported; no adapter, dual decoder, probe, window, bootstrap, or dependency. Future work is deliberately not created here: one bounded Orbit-owner slice in the next authorized ORBS revision, followed by separately owned Venus adoption and later Eon/Eonova pinning. Evidence, exact bytes, alternatives, first check, effort/risk, and reversal condition are recorded in the append-only decision comments.

comments.text:
Decision evidence and recommendation — pending explicit user selection; no implementation authorized.

Subject:
- Orbit HEAD 1446e64134489b6daad80f4a8e4514069122e027; AGENTS.md hash 095e3a9ea7e87d36f4ebabec1818ae42a4a4fce2.
- Current consumers inspected at Venus 4f799fef1c3e10e86d70b708708f7c2702d7aee8, Eon 01fbdd53c003688acb6d7e5461f36c83d8501f5a, and Eonova 247265c44f759f8142783af7dfd5415c25211c5c.
- Historical canonical ORBS sources/proofs: v1 838b67652c4df1979e599b9c401ee664ffac66bd, v2 9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757, v3 3ee7c80005f3d2bbe81e539799327803716f6174. Each validates its exact header VERSION before message kind or payload. orb-bi4.10, orb-j0m.3, and orb-ll1.1 selected exact, coordinated revisions; v1→v2 and v2→v3 used no adapter, dual decoder, probe, or compatibility window.
- The selected next ORBS work, orb-orbit-typed-wheel-outcomes-5nq, already specifies an owner-first breaking v3→v4 update with no compatibility layer. Deferred orb-j2i is serialized after this decision and after earlier protocol work.

Exact reproduction:
- Canonical v3 Hello 3..3: 4f 52 42 53 03 00 01 00 04 00 00 00 03 00 03 00.
- With only header bytes 4..6 changed to v2: 4f 52 42 53 02 00 01 00 04 00 00 00 03 00 03 00.
- The v3 decoder returns UnsupportedVersion { version: 2 } from the 12-byte header and never reads the still-compatible 3..3 payload.
- Canonical v3 Incompatible 3..3: 4f 52 42 53 03 00 83 00 04 00 00 00 03 00 03 00.
- With a v2 header: 4f 52 42 53 02 00 83 00 04 00 00 00 03 00 03 00. The v3 client likewise returns UnsupportedVersion { version: 2 } before decoding the typed response.
- Focused current check session::tests::framing_is_incremental_strict_and_bounded passed. The disposable v2-header probe passed both assertions.

Peer directions and current UX:
- Older client → current Orbit: Orbit rejects the old Hello header before its range. Its current-revision generic Failure, if written before close, is itself undecodable by the old client; EOF is also possible. No typed Incompatible crosses the boundary.
- Current Venus → older Orbit: the older server rejects the v3 Hello header under the same historical code shape. A response uses the older header or the connection closes. Current Venus maps an older response header to Lost with “unsupported local-session version N”; it cannot reach its typed Incompatible state.
- Venus sends Hello { minimum_version: VERSION, maximum_version: VERSION }. Venus pins the canonical protocol proof; Eon pins exact Orbit and Venus sources plus ORBS interface v3; Eonova pins that Eon graph. No supported independently upgraded mixed-revision workflow was found.

Complete shapes:
1. Exact framing + honest simplification (recommended). orbit_protocol::session::VERSION remains the sole wire-version owner. Keep one selected-revision decoder. In the next already-authorized breaking ORBS revision, retain Hello/Attached only as attachment ordering/acknowledgment and remove or narrow range/Incompatible fields so they make no cross-header claim. A reader that sees another header version diagnoses it locally, does not parse the payload, promises no typed cross-version response, and closes only that client. Allocation bounds stay unchanged; owned LOC and tests should decrease. Old revisions remain intentionally unsupported.
2. Reserve the current range types. One decoder and unchanged bounds, but dead fields, unreachable cross-header response semantics, and misleading tests remain. Rejected: it buys no supported behavior and increases later removal cost.
3. Stable bootstrap envelope. A permanently stable bounded bootstrap decoder would select a later session decoder and could return a mutually decodable incompatibility result. It adds a second lasting wire layer, compatibility rules, rollout tests, and a new promise. Introduced in v4, it cannot make existing v1-v3 peers understand it; it only helps later independently upgraded peers. Rejected absent a selected mixed-version workflow.

Recommended owner/failure/update policy:
- Owner: the fixed ORBS header version in the canonical Orbit protocol package.
- Failure: exact mismatch is a transport-level incompatibility observed by each reader; stop at the header, allocate no payload, parse no message, and make no cross-version response guarantee. Venus may present the observed and required versions from its local decoder error.
- Update order: prove Orbit/ORBS owner first; separately pin Venus to that exact proof; then update Eon’s component graph; then update Eonova’s Eon pin. The owner-first gap is intentionally incompatible. No old-revision support, adapter, probe, or window.
- Contract effect: this planning decision changes no indexed contract. A later implementation preserves and reproves ORB-C3 while the separately authorized feature Bead owns any product-contract change (currently proposed ORB-C8 for ORBS v4); no new contract ID is needed for dead compatibility fields.
- First falsifying check: encode a Hello whose payload names the current revision, mutate only its header to V-1, and prove both role-specific length decoders reject at exactly the header without producing a typed response; the consumer check must prove Venus reports the local version mismatch and does not enter typed same-header Incompatible.
- Effort/risk: S implementation when folded into the next authorized revision; low code risk, medium coordinated-rollout risk, net deletion expected, no dependency.
- Reversal condition: revisit a stable bootstrap only after the user selects a supported workflow where Orbit and Venus must upgrade independently and mixed revisions must interoperate or exchange a mutually decodable error.

Verification on the unchanged subject:

title: Decide whole PTY-session shutdown ownership
description:
## Contract Routing

This is a planning-only Orbit lifecycle-policy decision. It changes no ORB product contract, implementation, dependency, protocol, or compatibility promise by itself.

Consumer: a local user explicitly terminating an Orbit Session directly or through Eon/EonTerm.

Trigger: Orbit receives an accepted shutdown signal while its PTY session contains a HUP-ignoring job-control process group distinct from both the initial child group and the current foreground group.

Result: the user chooses whether explicit Session shutdown owns and reaps every process group in the PTY session or intentionally permits distinct groups to survive, with exact observable semantics and owner-routed proof.

Important failures: no accidental survivor under a successful full-stop claim, PID-reuse-prone broad scan, unrelated process termination, unbounded cleanup, duplicate Eon ownership, or silent expansion into machine-restart persistence.

Impact: MED. Decision effort: M. Implementation risk: HIGH. Confidence: HIGH.

## Why

Orbit currently signals only the initial child process group and one foreground-group snapshot. POSIX job control permits other process groups in the same session. A HUP-ignoring background group therefore survives a clean Orbit shutdown. The present ORB-C1 wording does not explicitly say whether full-session shutdown owns that group, so this is a contract choice before it is an implementation bug.

## Evidence

- `src/platform.rs:112-127`: shutdown sends HUP/KILL only to the initial child group and one `tcgetpgrp` result.
- Negative `kill` targets one process group, not an entire session.
- Closed audit `orb-audit-orbit-platform-t4s`, finding F3, at source `750490f40f348b66aa8809c66c40587ca8db741f`: a real shell enabled job control, ignored HUP, and started `sleep` in a distinct background group. After SIGTERM and clean Orbit exit, PID 337993 survived reparented to PID 1 until the audit killed it.
- Closed integration audit `orb-audit-orbit-integration-ur9` distinguishes this from Eon's SIGKILL bypass: this finding remains even after Orbit cleanup is allowed to run.
- Deferred `orb-decide-orbit-session-adoption-4hu` asks who hosts/adopts Orbit after Eon loss; it is related but does not decide explicit shutdown of all job-control groups.

## Reference Classification

Required:

- Current `AGENTS.md`, this complete Bead, ORB-C1 and adjacent lifecycle contracts, `docs/REFERENCES.md` process-lifecycle route, `docs/RATIONALE.md`, `docs/CRATES.md`, exact cleanup code/tests, and both audit records.
- Exact Linux/POSIX session, process-group, controlling-terminal, signal, and reaping semantics recorded by the platform audit.
- Exact Process Triage reference for observe-plan-apply, protected boundaries, staged action, and verification—without importing its general process-classification scope.
- Exact zmx, shpool, and abduco cleanup behavior only for the same explicit-session-shutdown question.

Comparison only:

- Current process-group cleanup.
- Kernel/session supervision mechanisms that can identify and verify only the owned Session processes.
- `orb-decide-orbit-session-adoption-4hu` and Eon `eon-choose-orbit-owned-shutdown-zmn` solely to keep lifecycle decisions coherent.

Rejected scope:

- `/proc` or process-name scans as authority, killing an entire user subtree, system-wide cleanup, remote/machine-restart persistence, a shared broker, new daemon, new dependency, or Eon-owned PTY cleanup.

## Decision Method

1. Re-run the exact distinct-background-group reproduction and record initial, foreground, background, session, and parent identities before and after shutdown.
2. Compare:
   - Explicit shutdown owns all process groups in the Orbit-created PTY session, with a verifiable platform mechanism and bounded escalation.
   - Explicit shutdown owns only direct/foreground groups and reports/document the permitted survivor semantics honestly.
   - A supervisor/cgroup-hosted shape only if safe whole-session cleanup cannot be expressed within Orbit's current process authority.
3. For each shape, name the user-visible Stop result, owner of discovery/identity/signal/reap/timeout, ORB-C1 effect or new-contract need, Eon/EonTerm consequence, Linux/macOS replacement shape, failure modes, owned LOC, and first check.
4. Prefer no new process/dependency. Reject broad scans and duplicate Eon cleanup.
5. Stop for the user's explicit lifecycle-policy choice.
6. If full-session cleanup is selected, create one bounded Orbit implementation Bead and make any Eon acceptance work consume its proof.

Portability disposition: isolated platform dependency; the policy should be platform-neutral, while Linux and macOS need independently proved process/session mechanisms.

## Scope

In scope:

- Explicit shutdown semantics for PTY-session job-control groups.
- Contract/owner/update-order decision and first real process proof.
- Relationship to same-boot adoption and Eon cooperative shutdown.

Out of scope:

- Code/docs/contracts edits, implementation children, supervisor-crash adoption, remote/machine restart, persistence, socket races, transient EIO, or stopping existing user Sessions.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The exact survivor is reproduced and all relevant process/session/group identities are recorded.
2. The decision states whether accepted explicit shutdown permits or forbids distinct background-group survivors.
3. One owner is named for identity, enumeration, signaling, escalation, reaping/verification, timeout, and result reporting.
4. Full-session, permitted-survivor, and supervisor-hosted fallback shapes are compared without assuming a new daemon or dependency.
5. The decision names ORB-C1/new-contract implications, Eon/EonTerm effects, exact consumer update order, portability disposition, first check, effort/risk, and reversal condition.
6. Broad PID/process-name scans, Eon-owned cleanup, unrelated-process killing, and unbounded waits are rejected.
7. No implementation or contract change occurs before explicit user approval.
8. Only this planning record changes; related decisions are linked without false blocking dependencies.

## Verification

- Re-run the isolated HUP-ignoring background-group reproduction without repository edits and clean every spawned process.
- `rg -n 'stop_and_reap|tcgetpgrp|kill\(|install_shutdown_signals' src tests docs` should enumerate local ownership.
- `git diff --check` should pass on the unchanged repository.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only planning state.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the current process/session topology no longer reproduces.
- Stop before selecting or creating implementation without the user's lifecycle-policy choice.
- Stop if the selected shape requires a new supervisor, dependency, compatibility promise, or contract not explicitly approved.
- Stop if another active issue owns the same shutdown-policy decision.

## Maintenance Notes

This decision is narrower than same-boot adoption: it applies when Orbit is intentionally shutting down. It is also deeper than Eon's SIGKILL bypass: cooperative Eon shutdown is insufficient if Orbit's accepted cleanup may still strand owned work.
notes: Accepted 2026-08-14: full explicit Session stop forbids survivors. Orbit owns bounded graceful shutdown, Linux per-Session containment escalation, empty verification, and result reporting; Eon only orchestrates. Preserve ORB-C1 and add one explicit shutdown contract in a separate owner-first implementation Bead. macOS remains blocked pending an independently proved containment replacement.

comments.text:
Decision evidence and recommendation — awaiting explicit user choice

Current evidence
- Candidate: edge 7c44105e09fc2a5e27f6ae6aee275e58198328fe on Linux 7.0.11-76070011-generic x86_64; target/debug/yazelix-orbit SHA-256 3ee6fa149ed6ac31a2f86acfc928d0b1534376396e92702786fca026c4386128.
- Isolated real-PTY reproduction used Bash job control and a background sleep that ignored HUP and TERM. Before shutdown: Orbit PID 1895292/PPID 1895264/PGID 1895264/SID 1895264; shell PID 1895294/PPID 1895292/PGID 1895294/SID 1895294; background PID 1895296/PPID 1895294/PGID 1895296/SID 1895294; foreground PGID snapshot 1895297. Orbit exited 0 and the shell was gone, but background PID 1895296 remained alive as PPID 1/PGID 1895296/SID 1895294. The harness then sent SIGKILL and verified it gone. No repository file was edited by the reproduction.
- Current owner path remains src/platform.rs:115-134: one initial-group target plus one tcgetpgrp snapshot, HUP then KILL, followed by direct-child kill/wait. The current lifecycle test proves only the initial shell and foreground child. Closed audit orb-audit-orbit-platform-t4s F3 at 750490f40f348b66aa8809c66c40587ca8db741f independently recorded the same survivor class. Eon's separate immediate-SIGKILL gap remains owned by deferred eon-choose-orbit-owned-shutdown-zmn.

Required reference disposition
- POSIX.1-2024 kill and terminal job-control semantics provide process and process-group targets, not a whole-session kill primitive. Negative kill therefore cannot make the current two-group snapshot complete.
- Linux man-pages 6.18 PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER confirms orphan adoption and wait ownership, while proc_tid_children explicitly says live-child enumeration is unreliable unless stopped/frozen. A subreaper plus /proc child traversal is therefore rejected as insufficient proof, even with pidfds; pidfds solve PID reuse, not complete enumeration.
- Linux cgroup v2 documentation provides the needed bounded identity: descendants inherit membership; delegated containment prevents escape; cgroup.kill handles concurrent forks/migrations; cgroup.events populated=0 verifies no live member remains. cgroup.kill is SIGKILL-only, so Orbit must retain a graceful bounded first phase before escalation.
- Process Triage d98c440e13b35fead5ad6b9ed10ed0baf72dc430, especially action/signal.rs and action/executor.rs, supports identity revalidation, staged action, bounded verification, and explicit outcomes. Orbit accepts those mechanics only; it rejects host-wide collection, classification, policy, and /proc scanning.
- FrankenTerm c0e586ff2f161c9426a9230859c355d4bd15ed44 confirms targeted child-tree visibility and staged verification are useful, but its Linux /proc traversal and macOS pgrep traversal are comparison evidence, not complete shutdown authority.
- zmx bea5fe315ca5fcd67f393cef9c8c2b0a6903ebca sends HUP then KILL only to the initial negative PID and waits the direct child; shpool 901e18c3ced010073178b78c0ca2a8cdd43e8581 sends HUP then KILL only to the child PID; abduco 8c32909a159aaa9484c82b71f05b7a73321eb491 exits and unlinks its socket while reaping reported children. These are useful bounded-cleanup comparisons but none proves the distinct-group case, so Orbit must not copy their scope claim.

Compared policy shapes
A. Full explicit Session stop within current PTY/session authority. Result: no distinct job-control group may survive an accepted stop. Current POSIX group/session primitives cannot enumerate and atomically terminate the owned set; a SID or process-name scan has PID-reuse, fork, setsid, and unrelated-process races. The policy is desirable, but this direct implementation shape is rejected. Estimated implementation M-H and correctness risk HIGH; no honest first check can pass without a stronger containment identity.
B. Permitted survivor. Result: Stop means Orbit, the initial group, and one foreground snapshot stop; HUP-ignoring distinct groups may remain under PID 1. Orbit would own the limited targets, deadline, direct-child reap, and honest non-full result; Eon and EonTerm would never compensate. This is approximately S work and LOW implementation risk, but creates surprising resource leaks and makes a successful user-visible Session stop weaker than its name. First check would deliberately assert the survivor. Recommendation: reject.
C. Full stop through platform containment. Result: accepted explicit Session stop forbids every live Orbit-owned descendant from surviving, including distinct process groups and descendants that call setsid. A Linux platform host supplies one delegated, per-Session cgroup before PTY exec; descendants inherit it. Orbit remains outside that kill target and is the sole lifecycle/result owner. Orbit performs its existing graceful PTY/group phase, waits a fixed deadline, uses cgroup.kill only for remaining members, reaps its direct/adopted children, and reports success only after cgroup.events says populated=0. Kernel cgroup membership owns identity/enumeration; the platform seam owns signal mechanics; the Orbit owner loop owns policy, grace/escalation timing, reap/verification coordination, exit result, and error reporting. Eon owns only orchestration. Estimated implementation H and risk HIGH, primarily delegation/launch atomicity, stuck D-state behavior, and packaging availability. This is the recommendation.

Contract, consumer, and portability consequences if C is approved
- Preserve ORB-C1: it still governs survival while Orbit remains running. Add one explicit shutdown contract rather than stretching ORB-C1; allocate its ID only after approval. Success means zero live members by the deadline. Inability to establish containment must fail before PTY spawn; inability to empty/verify it must produce bounded non-success, never a false clean stop.
- Owner-first order: (1) one Orbit implementation/proof bead establishes Linux containment and the new contract; (2) Eon eon-choose-orbit-owned-shutdown-zmn selects cooperative signal-driven shutdown against that exact proof, waits boundedly, and reports failure rather than duplicating PTY cleanup; (3) EonTerm/Venus consumes only Eon's stop result. Pin the exact Orbit proof; no old-version fallback, adapter, or compatibility window. Same-boot adoption remains separate.
- First contract check: start a real job-control shell with an initial group, foreground group, and HUP/TERM-ignoring distinct background group inside the owned containment plus an unrelated sibling outside it; request shutdown; assert Orbit exits success before the deadline, all contained PIDs/groups are gone and membership is empty, the direct child is reaped, and the unrelated sibling remains alive. One forced containment-unavailable case must fail before child spawn.
- Portability: isolated platform dependency. Linux has a credible cgroup-v2 mechanism. Current macOS launchd documentation kills remaining processes only in the job's process group and therefore does not prove distinct-group cleanup; no public, verified per-Session descendant containment plus empty-notification replacement was found. Record this as a macOS blocker with estimated HIGH removal cost and make no macOS runtime claim. Do not weaken the platform-neutral policy to obtain apparent portability.
- Reversal: choose B only if the product intentionally wants explicit Stop to permit orphaned work. Revisit containment only if a smaller kernel/supervisor mechanism proves complete membership, bounded termination, and empty verification without a new daemon or broad scan.

Explicitly rejected in every shape: broad PID/process-name/SID scans as authority, killing a user/system subtree, Eon-owned group discovery or cleanup, unbounded waits, false success after escalation failure, a new daemon, a dependency without a Crate gate, and machine-restart persistence.

Recommended user choice: C — full explicit Session stop, no survivors, implemented owner-first through Linux platform containment. No implementation bead, contract edit, dependency, or code change is authorized or created by this record.

title: Define Orbit same-boot management contract
description:
## Outcome

Define the smallest user-visible Orbit lifecycle-management contract for the same-boot Eon-supervisor-loss guarantee approved in `orb-decide-orbit-session-adoption-4hu`. The contract must be precise enough for the user to approve, revise, or reject before any contract-index or implementation edit.

Consumer: one replacement local Eon supervisor.

Trigger: the prior Eon supervisor disappears on the same boot and login while the exact Orbit process remains alive.

Result: the replacement validates the exact owner-authored Orbit Session and run identity, acquires the sole management lease, and reaches the unchanged PTY and authoritative terminal state through canonical ORBS. Explicit stop routes through Orbit and retains ORB-C12 cleanup semantics.

Important failures: stale or replaced endpoints, wrong Session or run identity, wrong user, incompatible generation, partial startup, concurrent replacement, Orbit exit, endpoint loss, logout, reboot, and machine loss fail with bounded non-success and cannot authorize PID, pathname, process-name, cgroup, or pidfd fallback.

## Contract routing

This planning-only decision changes no ORB-C, EON-C, or VEN-C contract, reserves no contract ID, and authorizes no code, test, manifest, package, service, binary, crate, protocol, or `docs/CONTRACTS.md` edit.

Preserve ORB-C1 through ORB-C12. Orbit remains the PTY, libghostty state, child-exit, terminal-query, presentation, and contained-stop owner. Eon remains logical Session identity, run creation, topology, and recovery-policy owner. Venus remains transient. Management must remain separate from the one-client ORBS presentation attachment.

A later Orbit implementation bead may assign the next available ORB-C ID and index the user-approved contract before code. Eon consumption and cross-repository acceptance remain separate later beads.

## Scope

Draft exact lifecycle states, identity fields, control ownership, bounds, permissions, exit-status reporting, cleanup, portability, proof, and reversal conditions. Reconcile the draft against current Orbit and Eon owners plus the exact decision evidence recorded in comment 607 of `orb-decide-orbit-session-adoption-4hu` and the closed Eon decision `eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf`.

Out of scope: implementation; machine-restart persistence; topology storage; remote access; multiplayer; terminal snapshots; raw PTY replay; service-manager adoption; shared broker; double-fork launcher; public protocol; new dependency; and compatibility window.
design:
## Proposed contract

### Observable contract

Consumer: one replacement local Eon supervisor, acting independently for each Orbit run.

Trigger: the prior Eon supervisor disappears on the same boot and login after Orbit has published Ready, while that exact Orbit process remains alive.

Result: the replacement validates the exact owner-authored logical Session and run, acquires its sole management lease, and may attach through canonical ORBS to the unchanged PTY and authoritative terminal state. Explicit stop remains Orbit-owned and preserves ORB-C12.

Failures: incomplete startup, stale or replaced records or endpoints, wrong Session or run identity, wrong UID, incompatible record, component, or management generation, concurrent replacement, Orbit exit, endpoint loss, logout, reboot, and machine loss fail closed. No file, PID, process group, process name, cgroup, pathname, or pidfd can authorize attach or stop without the live Orbit handshake.

This contract recovers one live Orbit Session. It does not store or reconstruct Eon workspace, tab, pane, selection, or launch topology. Any topology shown after recovery is a separate Eon-owned decision.

### Lifecycle states

- Starting: Orbit has published no record and receives no adoption guarantee. A partial or failed startup is not adoptable. Orbit owns its startup cleanup; existing launcher rollback before Ready remains outside this recovery contract.
- Ready, unleased: Orbit is live, its atomic discovery record is present, and no management connection owns control. The PTY and any ORBS presentation client continue.
- Ready, leased: exactly one validated Eon connection owns management. Losing that connection returns Orbit to Ready, unleased without stopping the Session.
- Stopping: an accepted stop is committed and cannot be cancelled by manager disconnect. Orbit admits no replacement lease, runs ORB-C12, and reports success only after ORB-C12 succeeds.
- Ended: after the PTY child is reaped and the terminal lifecycle result is known, Orbit replaces the live record with one terminal tombstone, removes only its exact endpoints, and exits.
- Lost: if Orbit crashes or a live endpoint is lost, any remaining record is only stale evidence. Eon may quarantine it after ownership and type checks, but cannot infer a live owner or signal a candidate.

### Start, identity, and discovery

Eon supplies one non-empty logical Session ID and one fresh opaque run ID, each at most 128 UTF-8 bytes. Orbit binds both to its process lifetime. IDs are protocol values, not path components, secrets, or standalone authority.

Eon launches Orbit without parent-death coupling or Eon-owned stdio pipes. Management handles are close-on-exec and are not inherited by Venus, the PTY child, or descendants. After Ready, Eon exit or closure of Eon-private descriptors cannot stop or hold Orbit open. This requires no double fork, broker, service manager, new binary, or retained project log.

Orbit creates one canonical ORBS presentation endpoint and one private management endpoint beneath the accepted UID-owned runtime directory. After both listeners, the PTY child, and authoritative terminal state are ready, Orbit atomically publishes one versioned live record of at most 4 KiB. The record contains only its schema generation, logical Session ID, run ID, both endpoint locators and identities, Orbit component generation, management protocol generation, process ID, and opaque process-start identity. The record locates and corroborates a candidate; it grants no authority.

Eon considers an initial start or replacement adoption successful only after a live handshake. Both peers require the expected UID. Eon also requires the record fields, logical Session ID, run ID, exact component and management generations, process ID and start identity, and endpoint identities to remain unchanged through the handshake. A mismatch is definitive and precedes any control grant. The management surface never returns terminal content.

### Management lease and presentation

Orbit permits one management connection per run. The validated connection is the lease. Two Eon supervisors may race; Orbit grants one lease and returns Busy to the loser. Disconnect releases a Ready lease without stopping Orbit. Disconnect after an accepted stop does not cancel shutdown.

The lease supports only bounded identity, live status, and explicit stop requests, with one request and one response in flight. It cannot read ORBF frames, send terminal input, resize, select, copy, or answer terminal queries. Canonical ORBS retains its separate one-active-presentation-client rule and ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 behavior. Venus has no lifecycle role.

Explicit Eon stop must use the validated lease. Orbit executes ORB-C12 and returns success only after its accepted containment, reaping, verification, and cleanup conditions succeed. If validation or transport fails, Eon reports non-success and does not signal through another handle. The live Session remains unchanged unless Orbit had already accepted stop.

### Terminal status and cleanup

After a natural child exit, or after a successful explicit stop has reaped the child and completed ORB-C12, Orbit atomically replaces the live record with one terminal tombstone of at most 4 KiB. It contains the record schema generation, logical Session ID, run ID, Orbit component generation, management protocol generation, process-start identity, termination reason, and exact typed wait outcome: exit code or terminating signal. It contains no attach or stop authority.

A client that loses a stop response reconciles through the remaining live handshake or the tombstone; it never retries through an external signal path. Eon removes a valid tombstone after reconciliation. The same-boot runtime owner removes unreconciled remnants when that runtime ends. A corrupt, oversized, wrong-owner, wrong-mode, symlinked, or newer record is rejected and may be quarantined as inert evidence.

Orbit stores no terminal frames, scrollback, graphics, argv, environment, credentials, process memory, topology, or project-owned retained log. A same-UID process can read or replace same-user state and can race for the lease; this lifecycle contract is not a sandbox between processes running as the same user. Live owner validation still prevents stale metadata from becoming authority.

### Bounds and permissions

- Eon bounds initial start and replacement recovery to one five-second operation. It retries only transient connection unavailability within that deadline. Identity, ownership, permission, generation, malformed-record, and Busy results are definitive for that attempt.
- Orbit bounds an incomplete management handshake to one second, each management message and each live record or tombstone to 4 KiB, each identity to 128 bytes, error detail to 1 KiB, and work to one request plus one response in flight.
- Orbit emits at most one live record or tombstone for its run. Eon owns enumeration, scan limits, and cleanup across runs; this Orbit contract sets no global record-count ceiling.
- Runtime directories are exact 0700 UID-owned directories. Sockets and regular records are exact 0600 UID-owned objects. Consumers reject symlinks, unexpected object types, wrong UID, group or other access, endpoint replacement, and size overflow before use.
- A silent, slow, malformed, or disconnected manager cannot block PTY processing, ORBS publication, child observation, or shutdown.

### Portability

Logical Session and run identity, record and message values, lease state, status, and failure meanings are platform-neutral. Spawn and stdio independence, peer credentials, process-start identity, endpoint identity and permissions, polling, and optional pidfd corroboration stay behind the platform seam. Linux is the first proof target. Linux proof grants no macOS support claim. Logout survival requires a separate product and platform decision.

### First proof

Launch one deterministic long-lived PTY command through Eon and record the exact Eon, Orbit, PTY child, Session, run, endpoint, and terminal identities. Kill Eon with SIGKILL without signaling Orbit. Prove useful work, the same Orbit and PTY child identities, and authoritative terminal state continue. Prove that no management or Eon-private descriptor inherited by Venus or the PTY child prevents lease release.

Start two replacement controls. Prove one acquires the same live run and the other receives Busy. Attach through canonical ORBS to the same terminal revision, request stop through the lease, and prove ORB-C12 empties the exact containment, the terminal tombstone reports the typed outcome, and no exact endpoint remains.

Authority negatives cover wrong Session and run IDs, stale and replaced endpoints, wrong UID and modes, symlinks, incompatible generations, malformed and partial records, silent or pressured management peers, Orbit exit during recovery, and a tombstone without lifecycle authority. Lifecycle negatives prove that a copied or stale record cannot recover after Orbit loss or a fresh runtime; logout, reboot, and machine survival remain explicit non-claims.

### Selection and reversal

Select the existing per-Session Orbit with one private management lease. Retain current behavior as the no-change reversal. Reject a double fork, shared broker, service-manager requirement, new binary, new direct crate, public protocol, retained log, and PID or path adoption for this slice. A pidfd may only corroborate a validated Linux process.

Reconsider systemd or launchd only if logout, start-at-login, or administrator supervision becomes required. Reconsider a broker only if the owner proof shows that one Orbit cannot provide exact status and a sole lease with less total machinery. Reverse to current parent-only behavior if proof requires unsafe PID or pathname authority.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The Bead records one exact proposed contract with consumer, trigger, result, and important failures, and assigns no contract ID before user approval.
2. Ownership is singular: Eon owns logical Session identity, run creation, topology, enumeration, cleanup policy, and recovery policy; Orbit owns PTY, terminal state, child wait status, management lease, presentation, and contained stop; Venus owns no lifecycle state.
3. The guarantee begins only after Orbit atomically publishes Ready. Starting, Ready unleased, Ready leased, Stopping, Ended, and Lost states have explicit transitions and failure results.
4. Recovery applies independently to one live Orbit run and explicitly does not reconstruct Eon workspace, tab, pane, selection, or launch topology.
5. The live handshake validates logical Session ID, run ID, exact record, component, and management generations, process ID and start identity, endpoint identities, and both peer UIDs before control. Records and process metadata remain locators or corroboration.
6. Management remains separate from canonical ORBS. Disconnect releases the sole Ready lease without stopping Orbit, an accepted stop is not cancelled by disconnect, and a concurrent replacement receives Busy. ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 remain unchanged.
7. Eon-owned stdio and management descriptors cannot couple Orbit lifetime or leak into Venus, the PTY child, or descendants. No double fork, broker, service manager, retained log, binary, or crate is required by the contract.
8. Explicit stop uses only the validated lease and preserves ORB-C12. Failure to validate or connect returns non-success and authorizes no PID, process-group, pathname, process-name, cgroup, or pidfd signal fallback.
9. A versioned bounded tombstone records one ended known run after natural exit or successful explicit stop, including termination reason and exact exit-code-or-signal outcome, but grants no attach or stop authority. Atomic transition, retention, deletion, corruption, and uncertain-response reconciliation are explicit.

11. The permission model covers exact directory, socket, and record modes; object type; peer UID; symlinks; endpoint replacement; stale state; and same-UID limits. A slow or malformed manager cannot block the Orbit owner loop.
12. Graphical-client loss, Eon loss, explicit stop, child exit, Orbit loss, endpoint loss, deliberate lifecycle handoff, logout, reboot, and machine loss have distinct outcomes.
13. Neutral contract values and state are separated from Linux process and socket mechanics. macOS receives no support or logout claim from Linux proof.
14. The first proof preserves useful PTY work and identity across Eon SIGKILL, proves management handles are not inherited, gives one of two replacements the lease, attaches through canonical ORBS, and completes owner-routed ORB-C12 stop. Negative checks cover every authority path and stale-state class.
15. No change, systemd or launchd, shared broker, per-Session Orbit, pidfd, and PID or path adoption are selected, rejected, or conditional with reversal evidence.
16. The user approves, revises, or rejects this exact text before closure. Closure changes no product contract or index. A later owner implementation bead assigns the next available ORB-C ID and indexes the approved contract before code; Eon consumption and cross-repository acceptance remain separate.

title: Evaluate a Bend2 proof model of Orbit attachment semantics
description:
## Contract routing

This is a bounded research and decision spike for an external proof model. It changes no ORB product contract and does not authorize a Bend2 runtime dependency, production rewrite, generated C/CUDA integration, permanent proof directory, hosted CI job, protocol/schema copy, or change of implementation language. The Rust Orbit implementation and indexed contract proofs remain authoritative.

The first experiment models only the cohesive ORB-C1/ORB-C4/ORB-C7 attachment-and-revision cluster. Selection, terminal semantics, wire encoding, PTY syscalls, graphics, persistence, and Venus are excluded. A successful result may justify a separate user-approved adoption or expansion Bead; it does not widen itself.

Impact: potentially medium if Bend2 expresses a small readable machine-checked lifecycle invariant. Effort: M. Risk: high because Bend2 is unreleased and an external model has an unavoidable refinement gap from Rust. Confidence: medium that the spike can reach a useful adopt/reject decision, low that it should become production infrastructure.

## Current state and evidence

As of 2026-08-11, the public `VictorTaelin/Bend2` repository reports `Bend2 - WIP`, has no commits or license, and cannot supply an inspectable proof language. Do not begin from announcements, private demonstrations, Bend1, or inferred syntax. Begin only from a public exact Bend2 release or commit with source, license, proof semantics, documentation, and a reproducible toolchain.

Orbit evidence:

- `docs/CONTRACTS.md` defines ORB-C1 client-independent PTY lifetime, ORB-C4 complete-frame attachment plus strictly ordered revisions, and ORB-C7 bounded slow/broken-client behavior.
- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs:338-367` owns strict complete-frame revision reduction.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:562-598` owns bounded role-specific attachment framing before payload buffering.
- `src/main.rs:236+` keeps the authoritative revision in the single owner loop.
- `src/main.rs:1061-1075` owns checked revision advance and detach-side selection cleanup.
- `tests/lifecycle.rs` and `src/presentation.rs` provide the executable real-PTY traces that any abstract model must map to without replacing.

## Prerequisites

- This Bead remains deferred until the user selects it and Bend2 satisfies the public-source gate. Model the current accepted post-ORBS-v3 proof at `6de95296d252c119d4fdba2d9b03cec1a09355ae`; closed `orb-ll1.1` is historical provenance, not an active blocker.
- Bend2 must have an inspectable public source revision or release, an explicit license compatible with this research use, official language/proof documentation, a reproducible Linux toolchain, and a way to verify proofs non-interactively.
- Do not start while another issue or agent changes the selected Orbit state-transition surface.

The Kani and Verus evaluation Beads are comparison evidence only and are not sequencing dependencies.

## Required references before model code

Required: current `AGENTS.md`; exact accepted ORB-C1, ORB-C4, and ORB-C7 proofs; the complete accepted owner-loop attachment/detach/frame/pressure paths and their real-PTY tests; `docs/CRATES.md`, `docs/REFERENCES.md`, and `docs/RATIONALE.md`; exact public Bend2 source, license, compiler/runtime, proof checker, trust model, totality/consistency claims, numeric and linear/resource semantics, FFI/extraction behavior, supported platforms, and official examples at one immutable identity.

Comparison only: the sibling Kani and Verus spikes, Lean/Agda-style external models, and Bend1/HVM history. Rejected: treating creator claims as proof semantics, importing Bend1 behavior, or copying Orbit Rust into a second executable implementation.

If repository production code, tests, manifests, docs, generated files, or configuration would be edited, first claim this non-epic Bead, record the execution baseline, and pass the evidence-first gate. Any tool/dependency or manifest change requires the full crate/dependency gate and user approval. Hosted automation requires a separately justified CI contract.

## Smallest model

Define a finite, explicit transition system independent of terminal cell contents:

- State: PTY/session liveness, zero-or-one attached client, authoritative revision, whether the attachment's initial complete frame has been emitted, and bounded client-output disposition.
- Events: attach attempt, complete initial frame, authoritative frame publication, client detach/failure, output pressure, PTY close, and shutdown.
- Observations: attachment outcome, complete-frame revision, disconnect/failure, and PTY/session liveness.

Prove only:

1. At most one client owns attachment in every reachable state.
2. Client detach/failure never changes a live PTY/session to dead.
3. A successful attachment cannot expose a later revision before its coherent initial complete frame.
4. Every later exposed frame revision is strictly greater than the previously exposed revision.
5. Bounded client-output pressure disconnects/fails that client without creating a second attachment or unbounded modeled history.

Use the smallest numeric domain sufficient to expose ordering mistakes, then state exactly whether Bend2 proves the invariant generically or only for the finite bound. Include one intentionally invalid transition or inverted theorem and demonstrate that Bend2 rejects it.

Do not model ORBF/ORBS bytes, terminal cells, libghostty, PTY/syscall behavior, selection, effects, viewport, search, graphics, persistence, multiple sessions, multiple clients, remote transport, Eon/Venus policy, or performance.

## Method and decision

1. Pin the exact accepted Orbit subject and exact Bend2 identity.
2. Record Bend2's trusted computing base, proof-checking semantics, consistency/termination boundaries, axioms/unsafe escapes, numeric semantics, and whether executable evaluation can diverge from proofs.
3. Build the model in a temporary isolated location with no Orbit manifest or source changes. Record its complete hash, owned LOC, command, duration, memory, assumptions, and proof output.
4. Map each modeled state/event/observation to exact Rust symbols and real-PTY tests. Name every behavior abstracted away; do not claim refinement between Bend2 and Rust.
5. Mutate one transition or theorem so the checker fails for the expected reason.
6. Compare proof clarity, coverage, maintenance, agent readability, toolchain/CI cost, and refinement gap with no external model and any completed Kani/Verus evidence.
7. Close with adopt, defer, or reject. Adoption means only that a separate user-approved Bead may persist or automate the model.

## Acceptance

1. A public Bend2 release/commit, license, source, proof semantics, toolchain, trust boundary, and exact non-interactive verification command are recorded. If any is unavailable, the Bead remains deferred or closes rejected without model code.
2. The model contains only the declared attachment/revision state machine and all five invariants; owned model/proof LOC and duplicated concepts are counted.
3. Every modeled element maps to exact accepted Orbit Rust and contract evidence, while every abstraction and the Rust-to-model refinement gap is explicit.
4. The positive proof succeeds and one deliberate negative mutation fails for the intended reason at the exact pinned Bend2 revision.
5. Proof bounds, axioms, unsafe/trusted declarations, numeric assumptions, excluded events, command, duration, memory, model hash, and raw-result location are recorded.
6. No Bend2 code enters Orbit production, no generated artifact executes in Eon, no product schema or contract changes, and no ORB proof revision/status is updated.
7. Closure records adopt/defer/reject, comparison with no model and available Kani/Verus evidence, retained-value proposal if any, removal cost, and the required fresh user decision before persistence or CI.

## Verification

Against the unchanged accepted Orbit revision:

- `cargo fmt --check` exits 0.
- `cargo check --locked` exits 0.
- `cargo test --locked` exits 0.
- `cargo test --locked -p orbit-protocol` exits 0.
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings` exits 0.
- `cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .` exits 0.
- `git diff --check` exits 0.
- The exact release-supported Bend2 non-interactive proof command is recorded and proves the declared positive model while rejecting the deliberate negative mutation.
- `br sync --flush-only` persists only the research record.

## Stop conditions

Stop if Bend2 remains unpublished, lacks an explicit usable license or proof documentation, cannot verify non-interactively, requires a protocol mirror or production redesign, cannot express the transition system without trusted axioms that erase the invariants, or progress requires a repository, dependency, CI, compatibility, contract, or cross-repository change without fresh user approval.

title: Evaluate Kani for canonical Orbit protocol proofs
description:
## Contract routing

This is a bounded research and decision spike. It changes no ORB product contract and does not authorize a runtime dependency, permanent proof harness, hosted CI job, protocol/schema copy, or production refactor. Candidate evidence may assess whether Kani can harden the existing proofs for ORB-C3, ORB-C4, ORB-C5, ORB-C7, and ORB-C9, but it cannot change their indexed status or proof revision.

Impact: medium-high if Kani proves a security- or correctness-relevant property against canonical Rust. Effort: S-M. Risk: medium. Confidence: high that the experiment can reach a clear adopt/reject result.

## Why and evidence

- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs:320-335` owns checked ORBF size accounting and the 4 MiB bound.
- `crates/protocol/src/lib.rs:338-367` owns complete-frame reduction and strict revision monotonicity.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:562-598` validates ORBS magic, revision, flags, role-specific payload bounds, and minimum lengths before payload-sized buffering.
- `crates/protocol/src/session.rs:980-1007` owns bounded framing and exact-message rejection.
- `src/main.rs:1061-1065` fails explicitly when the authoritative presentation revision is exhausted.
- `docs/CRATES.md` records `orbit-protocol` as a private, dependency-free, platform-neutral owner with extensive finite tests; `orb-fuzz-orbit-codecs-kf5` separately plans fuzzing but does not provide exhaustive bounded proof.

The decision is whether Kani adds material confidence against the production Rust owner without duplicating its schema, weakening assumptions until the claim is empty, or imposing more toolchain/maintenance cost than the proved property is worth.

## Prerequisite

The user selected this actionable research spike on 2026-08-14. Its starting subject is canonical ORBS v4 and the current affected proofs: `2e41997cbec202afc5222f084ffb98973a01b0f0` for ORB-C3, ORB-C5, ORB-C7, and ORB-C9, plus `3991dbf861f55bf9ac445f50b6cacd0b3992a271` for ORB-C4. Closed `orb-ll1.1` is historical provenance, not an active blocker. Reconfirm the exact accepted revisions at execution, and do not start while another issue or agent changes `crates/protocol` or the selected proof surface.

## Required references before proof code

Required: current `AGENTS.md`; exact accepted ORB contracts and proof revisions; current `orbit-protocol` production code, tests, callers, `docs/CRATES.md`, and `docs/REFERENCES.md`; `orb-audit-orbit-protocols-bkk`; `orb-fuzz-orbit-codecs-kf5`; and Kani's official documentation and source at one exact release or commit, including supported Rust features, proof harness semantics, contracts, loop/unwind bounds, assumptions, soundness limits, license, and toolchain requirements.

Comparison only: current finite Rust tests and the planned fuzzing shape. Rejected scope: a handwritten Kani protocol model, alternate decoder, copied constants, or proof over a stub that removes the property under test.

If repository production code, tests, manifests, or generated files would be edited, first claim this non-epic Bead, record the required execution baseline, and pass the evidence-first gate. A direct/tool dependency or manifest change requires the full crate gate and user approval. Hosted automation requires a separately justified CI contract.

## Smallest experiment

1. Record the exact accepted subject revision and compare three shapes: current tests plus no new verifier; the accepted fuzzing plan; and exact Kani.
2. Select one smallest non-trivial property that exercises canonical production Rust. Preferred order:
   - every syntactically complete ORBS header either rejects before payload buffering or yields a length within the role-specific maximum;
   - checked ORBF/session size arithmetic cannot overflow into acceptance;
   - `FrameReducer` never replaces its current frame with an equal or older revision;
   - a bounded canonical encode/decode property if Kani can construct valid production values without a parallel schema.
3. Keep initial harness code outside production ownership and avoid manifest changes. Record every assumption, stub, unwind/loop bound, explored input domain, proof time, peak memory, and whether the property is bounded or unbounded.
4. Run one negative mutation or assertion inversion to demonstrate that the harness can fail for the intended reason.
5. End with adopt, defer, or reject. Adoption means only that a separate user-approved implementation Bead may be proposed; it does not retain candidate code automatically.

## Acceptance Criteria

The canonical criteria are stored in this Bead's `acceptance_criteria` field.

## Verification

Against the unchanged accepted repository revision:

- `cargo fmt --check` exits 0.
- `cargo check --locked` exits 0.
- `cargo test --locked` exits 0.
- `cargo test --locked -p orbit-protocol` exits 0.
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings` exits 0.
- `cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .` exits 0.
- `git diff --check` exits 0.
- The exact release-supported `cargo kani --harness <selected-harness>` command is recorded and either proves the declared property or produces the captured rejection evidence.
- `br sync --flush-only` persists only the research record.

## Stop conditions

Stop if the accepted subject changes, an active agent owns the surface, Kani requires a protocol mirror or production redesign, assumptions erase the relevant invalid-input space, the verifier cannot consume the canonical Rust subset, or progress requires a manifest, CI, compatibility, contract, or cross-repository change without fresh user approval.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The record pins exact Kani source/release, license, Rust/toolchain requirements, Nix/offline feasibility, supported target shape, and replacement/removal cost.
2. The candidate matrix compares no new verifier, fuzzing, and Kani on proof strength, false-confidence risk, owned proof LOC, build/CI time, maintenance, portability, and agent readability.
3. At least one meaningful property runs against canonical production Rust, or the exact language/library/tool limitation is reproduced and justifies rejection.
4. The proof record states its full input domain, assumptions, stubs, bounds, exclusions, command, duration, and counterexample behavior. A bounded result is never described as universal.
5. No second ORBF/ORBS schema, decoder, constants inventory, product behavior, compatibility surface, or runtime dependency is created.
6. Existing canonical tests remain the executable behavior oracle. The result cannot mark an ORB contract Proved, refresh its proof commit, or displace real-PTY/native evidence.
7. Closure notes record adopt/defer/reject, the smallest valuable retained shape if any, rejected alternatives, exact commands/results, and a user decision gate before durable adoption.
notes:
Research outcome: DEFER durable adoption. Kani 0.67.0 at 4feaaad1d6a2378a6ff6caa3b4fc5d6999c7bb5d proved the client and server ORBS v4 fixed-header length bounds against canonical production Rust for every 12-byte header, with no assumptions, stubs, copied schema, or unwind bound. The assertion inversion failed with a concrete valid client Key header, proving non-vacuity. Positive runs took 2.92 s and 2.63 s wall at about 250 MiB peak RSS; setup requires a 483 MiB Kani bundle plus a 2.2 GiB exact nightly. No product defect was found.

Ownership and code shape: orbit-protocol remains the sole codec owner; existing deterministic tests remain the behavior oracle; fuzzing remains the complementary variable-payload tool. No production, test, manifest, generated, contract, crate-index, README, CHANGELOG, CI, dependency, or retained proof-harness change was made. Owned repository LOC and dependency footprint are unchanged. Portability disposition: neutral protocol research, executed only on x86_64 Linux.

Smallest future retained shape requires a fresh user decision: only the two assumption-free fixed-header harnesses, exact Kani pin, opt-in local execution initially, and no retained negative harness. Reconsider after ORBS fuzzing, a header revision, an allocation-bound regression, or a repository-wide formal-tooling decision.

Verification at unchanged HEAD ef2b98c6867192ddb22e7d8629aa01ed862cedb7: cargo fmt --check PASS; cargo check --locked PASS; cargo test --locked PASS (21 unit and 13 lifecycle); cargo test --locked -p orbit-protocol PASS (18 unit); cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings PASS; git diff --check PASS. cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- . FAILS only on the pre-existing unknown ORB-C12 references in orb-1sd and orb-prove-no-survivor-session-shutdown-btg. This issue cannot honestly close until that repository-wide gate is repaired or the user approves a protocol exception. Full identities, matrix, raw result hashes, assumptions, bounds, limitations, and decision rationale are in the append-only comments.
close_reason: Research complete: the bounded Kani 0.67 trial proved the selected protocol property, while durable adoption remains deliberately deferred and canonical production behavior is unchanged. Orbit governance passes after correcting the stale planning-only ORB-C13 reference.
